First Discourse on Joseph

O Christ, the Beauty with which all the righteous adorned themselves, grant me to gaze in wonder at how beautiful you are. O great Image from which all beauties take their colors, look upon me, so that I may be filled with your splendor and speak of you. O glorious Sun from which the rays take their radiance, pour your radiance into me so that I may speak of your splendor. O great Deep from which all springs draw, let streams of your sweetness flow through me too. O Son in whom are hidden all beauties, grant me to recount the splendid beauty of one who was beautiful. Truth has required me to tell Joseph’s story. From you, our Lord, may I become rich and enrich whoever listens to me. An ugly man has been moved to speak of a beautiful one. Through you, my Lord, may the color of my speech become beautiful, though it is not bright. It is not because I am pure that something has stirred within me concerning that pure man. Rather, Truth demands what belongs to it, like a judge. Though I am not beautiful, Joseph’s beauty now urges me to tell through my words the ocean of his deeds in all its abundance. Unless I gaze upon you, Jesus, perfect Beauty, I cannot even attain a glimpse of Joseph’s beauty. Unless you, the Light, shine upon my thoughts, not even a ray will show me what he is like. In you all the beautiful have adorned themselves, each in their own form. Through you may the beauty of the discourse about that beautiful man be adorned. May your beauty shine upon the listeners and fill them with wonder, and through your splendor sweep them away into praise. May they see you, my Lord, both listeners and speakers, while both groups marvel at you, for you are without limit. Sustain the mind that is pregnant, so that it may bring you forth beautifully, and sweetly give drink to the ear that thirsts for your words. Joseph, the son of old age, was painted in your colors, and therefore the image of his beauty shone throughout the whole world. Your testimony, my Lord, was placed in him, as it is written, and because of it he subjected kings in their lands. The likeness of your image clothed his youth in its beauty, and therefore the ends of the earth marvel at how beautiful he is. That freeborn man who became a slave resembled you, and for this reason he gave sustenance to those in need. If your leaven had not been kneaded into him, bread could not have abounded in his hands for those who were hungry. Here let the discourse establish its conclusion, O listeners: Joseph’s beauty excelled only through our Lord. So let us now paint an image in divine colors—the portrait of the Son that Joseph is, as we have said. This, then, is the aim of the discourse as it proceeds: all beauties gather together around the Son. The boy was beloved, and his reputation was also beautiful. Jacob brought him up in these spiritual ways of his. He had been instructed by Israel in spiritual things, and for this reason he gathered understanding beyond measure. With that old man who zealously held the angel fast, he was brought up to attain the height of wisdom. In Haran, Reuben and all his brothers in Laban’s household were brought up by Leah amid that brutish way of life, where the name of gods was known, but not that of God, and the land was gripped by confused customs without knowledge. While Jacob went out to the flocks in innocence, his sons were growing up among pagans without understanding. But Joseph came into being and did not follow their customs. From his childhood he was brought up in a chaste way of life. The mystery depicted in him did not allow him to conduct himself He was in that wickedness in which the sons of the slave women were growing up. He fixed his mind intently on Jacob his father, and from him he learned how to live wisely. The patterns of the Son held his gaze fast on his father's virtues. He did not look this way and that, lest he become confused. He saw that his brothers' conduct was not good, and wisely brought their bad report to his father. That innocent man did not agree with those brutish men, and therefore he told Jacob about their deeds. There was spiritual harmony between him and his father, for they meditated on the matters of God's household. Jacob loved Joseph very much because of the beauty of the Son of God that dwelt in him. Truth compelled him to portray the crucifixion in him, and he made a tunic with long sleeves for him to wear. Out of love, Jacob made arms for the garment, to depict in his son the great cross of the Son of God. In a great mystery, he spread the sleeves over the boy, and as he clothed him, he stretched him out in the garment as though on a cross. He bore the sign on his right and on his left, in a garment with the outstretched arms of crucifixion. Along with the beauty Joseph put on through the tunic, his brothers' envy rose fiercely against him. The great image astonished them with its splendid beauty, and like those who crucified the Lord, they were consumed with jealousy against the beautiful one. Like the sun, Joseph's beauty shone upon those darkened men. They were dazzled by it and filled with fury, intent on extinguishing it. These colors of the crucifixion depicted upon him spread beauty over his youth among the company of his brothers. Righteous Jacob rejoiced greatly in the beauty upon him, for a great image gazed out at him from his splendor. The more the love of Jacob his father increased, the more his brothers' envy also grew stronger. Look, from this you will take material, O teaching, to uproot that ulcer of envy from your hearers. Anger concealed within the mind is a canker; unless love cuts it out, the soul is not healed. Anger ruins the whole order of virtues. Its work is murder, and when it does not kill, its restraint is forced. Anger disturbs the serene soul when it is stirred up. It pours its flavor over the thoughts, and they become steeped in it. It splashes its mud over understanding and stains it, and through it all impulses toward virtue are blinded. Anger entered, and understanding departed from the mind. Wrath awoke, and all wisdom fell asleep. Envy, like smoke to the eye, makes the soul blind; when it enters the soul, its sight is too dim to see clearly. Jealousy within the mind is a foul odor, and it cannot enter a pure soul without making it stink. Resentment in the heart is like a viper in the dust of the earth, and wherever it pours out its venom, death comes swiftly. Truly, fear a resentful person rather than a snake, and come near a dragon rather than an angry person. A wrathful person cannot succeed in his deeds, for his anger spills out and makes him transgress his duty. Flee from wrath if you wish to live rightly, for wrath destroys the wise, as it is written. A cloud hides the sun's radiance from sight; in the same way, anger deprives the soul of vision. Love has a clear and peaceful eye. Its gaze is straight and does not stray from what is right. The soul needs guarding, for it is clear. And wherever it falls into the hands of anger, anger tears it apart. Carefully shut all the gates on every side, and do not let anger enter it— your soul—lest it perish. Fury does not carry out your will when it enters the soul; something else springs from it that is not yours. Be master of your will, you who are freeborn. Do not let fury rise within you and do what you do not want. Leave your soul sitting in the quiet that is easy for you. Do not cast envy into it, which agitates and bewilders you. Do not become a slave to fury and submit to it, lest you become its worker, pouring out blood for strife. Envy is a weapon held ready against good things, and whoever puts it on knows nothing but doing evil. Envy committed a crime on earth from the beginning, for it is very intent on destroying things that are well ordered. It was envy that drove the first Adam out of Paradise, and he acquired a land of thorns with toil in place of kingship. Envy cast contention among brothers long ago, and it killed the beautiful Abel through Cain his brother. This worker cast trouble among the company of brothers and subjected the fine men of the house of Judah to its yoke. It seized upon the freeborn man with threats that he should become a slave. For to harmony it does not submit, wherever it is. Envy is accustomed to corrupting the love of brothers, for from the beginning it has been a murderer through its deceit. The Son of God it hung on the cross—and what more can I say? Here it brought all the work of its bitterness to its climax. For this reason too, it had always threatened the beautiful, so that it might destroy that beauty of the Son, if it could. Every day envy comes from the left against the right. Take care not to fill yourself with envy and incur guilt with the left. Whoever is hateful belongs to the left, for no one crosses over to the right except through love. This weapon is forged with zeal for the devil. Hate envy, for it is the enemy’s weapon. With these implements the son of destruction carries out his work: with fury and resentment, envy and deceit, and wickedness of heart. Therefore flee from fury as much as you can, for through it the soul is blinded, so that it cannot see what is right. Whoever envies cannot see straight; his sight is impaired, so that it turns toward the left. Envy brought those brothers, the sons of that righteous man, to a stumbling halt. As for you yourself, if it reaches you, what will it do to you? It brought the company of ten low in battle when it entered them, and cast the eleventh into a pit in a deserted place. The wall of the brothers was breached by envy when it entered among them. It built a wall of anger in their midst and scattered them. If mighty men, the heads of the tribes, were defeated before it, where will you, weak as you are, end up if it rises within you? Envy in the heart is worse than a venomous snake in a hollow. Crush envy, lest through its venom you be destroyed. This is a passion that gives birth to death wherever it is, and its struggle is prolonged unless love drives it out. With this disease were afflicted all Joseph’s brothers, and they could not speak peaceably with him. It subdues the soul like a city when it enters it, and it carries out a raid within its precincts and lays them waste. It drives peace and tranquility out of the soul when it conquers it, and in anger the soul lies desolate, emptied of kindly thoughts. It drives love out and brings fury in to dwell there, for fury can destroy all the treasures of good things. “They could not,” it says, “speak peaceably” with him. Oh, how powerful is the force of envy! It corrupts all the soul’s impulses when it enters it, and throws the body’s limbs into confusion when it settles within it. It pours its gall over the mind and entangles it. It stains the face yellow and makes it gloomy. The soul is stained by it, becoming dark and estranged from righteousness. It covers up sound thoughts so that they cannot be recognized. Through it, the gaze of eyes that once looked straight becomes twisted, for whoever envies cannot look kindly. Evil envy turns the eye away from its proper state and makes its gaze hostile, so that it departs from what is fitting. Even the speech of the mouth it corrupts and confuses. It is utterly destructive of everything when it gains control. “They could not,” it says, “speak peaceably with him.” See, listener, that even speech was corrupted by envy. This is a disease for which there is no healing medicine: the more remedies you apply to it, the more it grows. Envy had entered the company of the righteous and entangled them, and they could find no way to escape their downfall. It fought fiercely against Reuben’s legion, and bound the whole of it with hateful resentment that gives birth to death. What could Joseph have done to heal them? For the more good things he did for them, the more it hurt them. The more he grew and excelled, the more their envy grew. By what means could they have been healed of their hatred? The more he took care to do good things, the more great pain was added to their pain. This is the sore that cannot be healed by anything, for the more you attend to its healing, the worse it becomes. Therefore, take care only that it does not arise within you, for if it does, no medicines can root it out. As long as it has not entered you, it is easy for you to see how bitter it is. But if it enters, you become stained by its ugliness. Give this evil passion no room to enter and corrupt your soul, which loves good things. Look and shudder at what it did to those brothers: whose sons they were, and what they did because they were envious. The sons of Israel—ten chosen men—hated one man. Envy had bound them and brought them low, though they had been blameless. Joseph was envied, and he did not know what to do. The more good he did, the more he was entangled by envy. And while envy barked at him every day from his brothers, revelation called him into the realm of dreams to speak with him. It drew him into sleep to tell him about hidden things, so that the hostile men who hated him would not frighten him. It cast sleep upon the boy whom his brothers envied, so that while he slept it might show him what was to come. For while he was awake, envy stood arrayed against the handsome young man; during sleep, it encouraged him with things to come. His brothers dishonored him, but dreams honored him through their revelations, so that he would not be distressed when envy assailed him every day. He entered the realm of hidden things and learned there that he was being given authority over all his brothers. The dream bound the ten who envied him, and through revelation subjected them to obey him. While he was asleep, they came, and his enemies became men bowing before him, so that he might take courage amid the waves they hurled against him. The dream raised him up and made him head over all his brothers, so that he might remain hopeful when he suffered dishonor at their hands. He was held in sleep and symbolically brought them into subjection, so that when he was enslaved he might bear in mind that he would be set free. The dream made them all bow down, and they worshiped him, so that this would be kept in his mind when he was humbled. It sustained him with the hope that he would be given authority, so that when he was sold he would not grieve over his slavery. The handsome young man slept, and the dream came and set out its revelations. When he awoke, he told the account to all his brothers, and they hated him still more because of it. He began to describe the dream he had seen and what it was: “Look, we were all binding sheaves in the field,” he said, “and my sheaf stood upright, and there were your sheaves bowing down to it. Mine was standing, while yours lay around it.” “Your dream is fine, if it is true!” they said to him. “You become a king through a dream, and you rule!” Envy concealed from them the truth, so that they could not see it. Though the dream had been interpreted, they denied it, even though it was true. Again another revelation called to Joseph and said to him, “You must not fear the resentful men who threaten you. They interpreted it well, though they hate you because of the dream. You will indeed rule, just as they told you.” Again the dream raised Joseph up in a revelation and made the heavenly powers and their courses bow before him. The sun and moon bowed their heads and worshiped him, for the heavenly lights saw the mystery of the Son in that handsome young man. The shining stars paid honor to the one clothed in mysteries, and from their places they worshiped him as their lord. Heaven and earth worshiped him through the sheaves and the heavenly lights. This belongs to the Son, whose dominion will have no end. Both day and night worshiped Joseph because they saw in him one clothed in the likeness of the great Sun of Righteousness. The dream ran, summoned the heavenly lights, and subjected them to the servant who wore his master's image, so that he might be honored through it. Night worshiped him through the moon and stars that bowed before him; day too honored him through the sun and its rays. The Son's death was depicted mystically in his sleep—the Son who shook all the heavenly powers when he suffered. Joseph was sleeping; as one might say, the Savior was dead. By his death he terrified the heavenly lights and shook them. In Joseph's sleep, the sun and moon worshiped him; at our Lord's death, all the heavenly lights were filled with terror. That son of Jacob lay stretched out in sleep as though on a cross, and his authority extended over the heavenly lights to command them. There he depicted the great death of the one who gives life to all, who shook both earth and heaven at his crucifixion. Joseph was asleep, just as our Lord was crucified, and the sun, moon, and all the heavenly lights bowed before him. Through the door of dreams the mystery entered and came to that chaste man. It visited him there on his bed and passed on and departed. In his sleep the heavenly powers ran and worshiped before him; at the Son's death all created natures were terrified. The image of the Son that was in Joseph, as we have said, received tribute from the heavenly lights and subjected them. The created sun, which people had gone astray and subjected themselves to, was subjected to Joseph in the dream through a great mystery. Our Lord's image received its due from the heavenly lights, so that their dominions would bow to its dominion. The likeness of Jesus was worshiped in the realm of dreams, for he is the ruler over created things in every world. Not even those who slept did the mystery deprive of its revelation, for he was ready to visit even the dead through his death. In the realm of sleep, dreams shone forth for Joseph. And in the place of the dead, the hidden worlds [?] concerning our Lord. His father and mother were bowing before him in the sun and moon. Eve and Adam, in that living Son, were rejoicing in him. Rachel had departed, and the dream comforted her because of Joseph. Eve had died, and the Firstborn visited her among the departed. The dream called Rachel from among the dead to bow before him—before Joseph, who kept his needy brothers alive during the famine. The reality truly called Eve to rejoice in him, in that living Son who descended and visited her among the departed. Amid these mysteries Joseph was sleeping, as you have heard, and dreams surrounded him to present him with their revelations. The first dream subjected his brothers’ sheaves to him, to show him that in his hands was food enough for all who were in need. And this second one extended his authority over the heavenly lights, to show him how high he would be raised to leadership. The earth’s produce bowed in its sheaves before that wise man, who was ready to provide well for his companions. The dream raised Joseph’s sheaf upright to show through it that, except in it, there was no food to satisfy those who were in need. The revelation cast down all the sheaves of Joseph’s brothers, but firmly set his own upright among its companions. For in it alone there was food enough, and not in the others. And because all these were in need, they bowed before it. In Joseph’s sheaf the revelation depicted the body of our Lord, from which were satisfied all the nations that longed for him. “I am the bread of life,” he said, “and whoever eats me will never hunger again, for in me there is satisfaction for those who are worthy of me.” This bread came down from on high to the hungry nations, and no other bread can satisfy except this one. Joseph’s sheaf was rising upright toward heaven to show where the bread that contains life is. As though with a finger, his sheaf pointed when it stood upright, indicating that above is the nourishment in which there is satisfaction. Both his dreams converged on a single mystery: why, in their different forms, they were bowing before him. The world below took the earth’s produce to present to him, and bowed before him with the heads of the sheaves, making supplication. Heaven brought all the rays and their heavenly lights, and it too bowed before the image it saw in that handsome man. For if Joseph had not been clothed in the image of the Son, neither the heavenly lights nor the world above nor the world below would have bowed before him. At the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, as it is written; those in heaven and those on earth shall obey him. Heaven and earth, in the dreams, were bowing before Joseph, for the mystery of the Son bent them down to obey him. Before Joseph’s bed the sun was bending down, and the moon was bowing, and they were worshiping him symbolically. At our Lord’s tomb this truly happened, for at his death a great light shone among the departed. The dreams paid honor to Joseph upon his bed, and within his tomb the angels likewise honored our Lord. The servant slept and saw in his dream that he would become a master, but our Lord died and by his death freed the race of slaves. Before whom did the sun bow during sleep except this man, upon whose beauty the image of the Son was visible? Before whose sheaf did the sheaves bow except his, in which the living bread of the Son of God was depicted? Joseph indeed slept and saw this second dream. When he awoke, he did not wish to conceal its story. The mystery of the night he revealed by day in the sight of many. He was not afraid of the envy that battered him every day. A dream spoke with him in his sleep and gave him strength, so that all the waves, when they battered him, would not distress him. He drew confidence from the revelation that was certain to him, and he stood up to recount the dream he had seen without anxiety. “Come,” he said, “and hear this other dream that I have seen: the sun and the moon, together with the heavenly lights, were bowing down to me. Eleven stars bowed their heads and submitted to me, and the sun and the moon lowered their rays before me.” Joseph understood the dream and its interpretations, and to beat down his brothers’ envy he was devising a way. It was as though someone were saying, “By God’s appointment, I am your head. Do not let what comes from the Most High distress you. Why am I envied by you because of Jacob’s love? God too has honored me in a dream, as I have recounted. The dream bowed even him down along with you, so that he would worship me. Why envy something that comes from God? Look,” he was telling them, “the sun and the moon bowed down to me, and the stars honored me. Why do you hate me?” With that account of the dream he recounted, he rebuked them for needlessly quarreling with him because he would become their head. He disclosed before them what God had appointed for the future, to put an end to their envy toward him. He told the dream as though he did not understand, although he did understand, so that when they knew, they would stop fighting. The wise man set the dreams of the night between himself and them, so that they would rescue him from those who envied him. He summoned revelation to stand before him like a judge and subdue the spiteful men who hated him. These visions seen in sleep he recounted before them, but they despised both him and the visions from God. He recounted the dream to his father in front of his brothers, and Jacob interpreted it while affirming it without making that known. He rebuked him while signaling to him to conceal the mystery, so that his brothers’ anger against him would not grow stronger because of the interpretation. “Will your mother and I really come, as you say, and your brothers with us, and bow down to you too? Is that what you think?” Jacob rebuked him while keeping all his words in mind, to ease the brothers’ envy for a while. As a deliberate tactic, he interpreted the dream as though he did not affirm it, until the time should arrive for what was destined to be revealed. His brothers were jealous of him and were filled with envious rage against him, while his father wisely kept all his words in mind. It tormented them— Joseph’s beauty—whenever they saw him, and every day it increased their pain, making them hate him still more. The dreams he had seen added to their anger against him, so that, before he became king, war was stirred up against the handsome young man. Every day jealousy chastised them because of Joseph, and they were tormenting themselves at all times. In envy itself there is something just: the one who envies is beaten and tormented as well. Envy knows how to inflict great suffering on its own people and to multiply blows, together with torment, for the one who possesses it. Look at this possession that produces pain for its possessors, this treasure of anger that is full of harm for the one who stores it up! Envy is in you, and look, it chastises you because you acquired it. You deserve to be beaten by it because you loved it. Let no one reproach the envious person, asking why he envies. His punishment is within him: envy, which hurts far more than rods. Whoever wishes to acquire a snake and live with him. What does he deserve except to be bitten by a snake? Whoever harbors envy, which is far worse than a snake, deserves to burn in that very envy. For it is right for the farmer, as it is written, to be the first to eat the fruits of his land. Envy, which is bitter—who tastes it except its owner? He planted the tree; let him eat its bitter fruits. Whoever harbors envy has his punishment within himself. No other blow needs to be brought against him. Though it is unjust, it is just in scourging the one who possesses it. It strikes not someone else but its own owner every day. Let us therefore flee from a possession that is nothing but punishment. Blessed is he who, through his love, drove envy away from the faithful. The first discourse on Joseph is finished.
The Second Discourse on Joseph
The Second Discourse on Joseph: When He Was Sent to His Brothers and They Threw Him into the Pit. By the Holy Mar Jacob.

Joseph’s story urges me to speak further about him. Even his name, like his story, calls for an addition. Let me therefore ask God with reverence that you, my Lord, may grant me more beauty for the discourse about that beautiful man. He is a great subject in whom truths are found, and in whom treasuries stand open, full of trustworthy things. Joseph bore an image of his Lord to bring into the world, and because of it everyone who encountered him bowed in honor before him. A radiance of mysteries he carried as he came from his father, and because of it he subjected lands and their inhabitants. A great likeness poured its beauty upon his youth, so that he would be honored with bowed heads while all who saw him marveled at him. The symbol of our Lord was handed down through all generations, and no one who was not worthy of it bore it. Isaac received it from Abraham as a faithful man and gave it to Jacob, who also shone and bore it with honor. Then Israel looked among the twelve to see who was worthy, and chose Joseph to be a tablet for the image of the Son. To him he entrusted the deposit that had been entrusted to him, which carefully he guarded like a wise man. Who was worthy to portray the sufferings except Joseph, who conquered passion and carefully guarded the members of his body? For whom was it fitting to bear the image of the Son of God: Reuben the firstborn, or Joseph, the eleventh? The one who went astray like water was not worthy, but rather this one whom the waters tested without his becoming wet. Simeon and Levi were instruments of wrath; how, then, could the image of the Son be portrayed in them, who loves peace? It was therefore fitting for it to be handed down through Joseph until Moses received it to bring it to the house of David. This image Jacob was eager to honor, for he saw that Joseph had received it from him and that it was firmly established in him. It was not by chance that he loved Joseph far more than his brothers, but because he saw the beauty of the mysteries in which he was clothed. For this reason he honored him as much as he could, to give his chastity its due, because it was pure. He saw that Joseph was unlike those ten in his deeds, and distinguished him from them by the tunic he made for him. The image of our Lord demanded its due from the righteous man: that he should prepare something new and present it to it. He prepared for him clothing different from that of his brothers, so that there might be depicted in him something new and unusual. He sent him to the flocks to visit his brothers, like the Son whom the Father sent to come and seek the sheep. who had gone astray. Old Jacob had entered into this mystery when he took his staff and fled from his father's house. He had not given it to Esau to bring it from Isaac, because the greedy man was not worthy to carry the image of the Son. Nor, here again, had he given it to Reuben the firstborn, because he was lax in turn, like Esau, who had become greedy. Resolute men bore the Son in honor throughout all generations, pure and chaste men who were worthy of him in their conduct. He chose zealous men to carry the great image, men whose thoughts reached high toward heaven: Isaac, who was bound to become a sacrifice at the hands of his father; Jacob, who carried the staff of mysteries and left his homeland; and Joseph, who stood firm against desire in his youth. These chosen men bore the King's image in honor. Jacob indeed saw who was worthy among the company of his sons. Through his hands he sent the image full of beauty into the world. He sent Joseph to visit the sheep, as we have said. This belongs to the Son, through whom the rational flock was saved. The well-being of his brothers was what Joseph was sent to see to, just as Christ spread peace along his whole way. But when Joseph came to the sheep as he had been sent, his brothers, whom he visited, did not receive him in peace. To whom had this ever happened except our Lord? He came to his own, and, it says, they did not receive him, although they were his own. Although Joseph had been sent to visit his brothers, they met him with murder, like those who crucified the Son of God. This road had been laid out from ancient times, and through their sufferings the righteous set up milestones of blood along it. Each of them labored on it as much as he could so that the mountain he had to cross would be made fair. Joseph set up many milestones along it, on the Son's road, which he traveled in purity and diligence. He made a great mountain easy to cross on the paths of crucifixion, traveling in anticipation along that road of blood. He brought his father's greeting of peace to his brothers and visited them, but they stirred up strife against him, like those who crucified the Lord. He was carrying provisions to bring his brothers from his father, just as Christ visited the earth with his healings. The wrongdoers took his provisions from him but did not receive him. This happened to our Lord, who gave healing and was treated with contempt. Look clearly, discerning people, at Joseph's road: in all its milestones it shines with the light of the Son's road. He brought peace, and he was met with anger, as you have heard. He visited the flock and found strife among the company of his brothers. He had come to Shechem to seek the sheep, as you have heard, but he did not find the flocks gathered there. The sheep had changed their location, in a great mystery, like humanity, which had strayed from the road of truth. How fitting it was for righteous Joseph to seek his brother's sheep with care in a desolate place! For he was depicting the Son of God in his mission, who sought humanity in the wasteland of idols, and it was found. Joseph had set out to travel along this road, and a bloody assault befell the young man, as it did our Lord. He sought the sheep until he reached the flock, and although it had moved away before him, he had not abandoned it. But when Joseph reached the sheep to visit his brothers, murderous strife was stirred up against the innocent man. Envy had seen him Joseph’s brothers saw from afar that handsome man, wrapped in mysteries, as he approached. He had [?] to visit his own amid great wrath. And fury poured from their mouths as they reviled him: “Here comes the dreamer! What shall we do to him? Today he must interpret his dreams and explain them to us. Let Joseph die because he imagined he would become king! Let us see what becomes of the dreams through which he exalted himself. Let us throw him into a pit, since he sought to seize leadership, and let us see his humiliation because he speaks so boastfully. Let his dreams come and rescue him, if they are true! In his sleep he became king, but awake, look, he is being enslaved! Deceptive dreams made him head over us all. Trample him, O heel, so that he no longer strides toward greatness!” Fury rose mightily against him, and while he was still far away, it prepared death for that handsome man. Envy had found a place to carry out its work, for there was no one to rescue him in that deserted place. Long-standing resentment displayed its strength when it emerged to commit murder and bathe in the blood for which it thirsted. Their daily bitterness poured there from their mouths, and its great reservoir wrought wickedness when it burst open. The resentful men saw Jacob’s heir, who had been sent, and plotted to put him to death so that he would not inherit. Here his likeness was absorbed into that of Christ, as though his were the suffering that befell Christ at the hands of the crucifiers. The farmers saw the owner of the vineyard, who had been sent, and, as with Joseph, they threatened him so that he would not inherit. “This is the heir! Come, let us kill him,” they plotted. “His inheritance too will become ours once we have killed him.” The Lord’s Son had been sent to the farmers, and they joined forces against him to kill him so that he would not inherit. For through the prophets he had been proclaimed from ages past, just as the dreams announced Joseph’s dominion to him. Fear of the dreams made Joseph’s brothers tremble, for unless he died, he would become king and exercise dominion. So too, from the revelations of prophecy, the people recognized that Jesus was the Father’s heir, and they contended for his death. “This is the heir,” they said, as it is written. “Come, let us kill him, and his inheritance too will be ours.” Joseph’s portrait closely resembles that of Christ, for all Christ’s sufferings were mystically depicted in it. “Here comes the dreamer! Let us throw him into a pit and see what becomes of his dreams, if they are true!” This resembles the mockery at Golgotha: “If you are the Son of God, save yourself!” The heads of the tribes laid up a treasure of ridicule for their children, and that mockery was passed down through their generations. From that inheritance of their fathers the crucifiers took their mockery of the Son who came to visit them. For the former said, “Let us see what becomes of his dreams,” and the latter, “Let him come down from the cross, and we will believe in him.” “Look, Elijah! Let us see whether he comes and rescues him.” This is the same as their saying, “Let the dream rescue him from us!” One meaning underlies these sufferings on both sides, for Joseph painted with the pigments of crucifixion. Great envy stood raised against him on the part of his brothers—the same envy that hung the Son of God upon the cross. The murderer who was intent on the Son’s killing had himself stirred up against Joseph: his brothers’ hostility. He had seen in Joseph a beautiful likeness of Christ, and he attacked him to shed the blood of the one he hated. It was not possible, however, for Joseph to undergo the great slaughter, for the sufferings and bloodshed were reserved for the Son of God. They threw him into a pit; he did not enter a tomb like our Lord. For if he had entered, he could not have come out by his own power. Sheol would have closed over Joseph if he had entered it, for he could not have torn down its walls like our Savior. He descended into the pit to see the shadow of death, for he was not capable of binding the mighty one in his own domain. If he had entered the city of death like our Savior, it would have shut its mighty gates against his departure. Had they directed his course to the tomb, like the Son of the Living One, he would have sunk into the chasm that swallows the dead. Had he entered the presence of Destruction to see its domain, through the ranks of worms that encountered him he would have decayed. Death would have lost nothing if Joseph had died, for its might was conquered only by our Lord. A servant could not tear down the walls of Sheol, for the city of death was conquered only by the Lord. If the freeborn Son had not entered the land of death, neither would freedom have been given to the race of slaves. For this reason Joseph did not die when he was sent, because the road of slaughter was not his to walk upon. He merely sketched it out, placed [?] upon it, and passed on, reserving the appointed bloodshed for the King, his Lord. The shadow of crucifixion fell upon him, the one who was envied, and confined him in the pit to open a tomb for his Lord who was coming. He could not descend and touch the bottom of Sheol, and for this reason he escaped the slaughter that was seeking him. They were plotting to kill him when he came, but the mystery spared him and gave him a pit instead of a tomb. Reuben the firstborn had been won over by truth to advise them: “It is not right for us to kill our brother and sink into his blood. Let us throw him into a pit, and let our hand not be against him, for even in the pit he will be brought low as though in death.” Brotherly love claimed its due through Reuben and found a way to rescue Joseph from the knife. For he had planned to save him, and that was why he gave this advice. His counsel prevailed, so that Joseph would live. This is an example for anyone who does good deeds: even if he sins, his good deeds are not disregarded. Reuben committed sexual sin, and Jacob excluded him from the number. But because he had planned good for Joseph, Moses brought him in. Israel broke Reuben’s staff because of his wrongdoing, but the good he had done stood before him and supported him. “You strayed like water; you shall not endure,” he said to him. But Moses declared, “Let Reuben live and not die.” Among the number of his brothers he placed him, because he had planned to save Joseph, whom they had prepared to put to death. His offense had driven him out from among his brothers; the good he had done was not disregarded by God. Let us therefore hasten to perform good deeds, for all of them are kept for justice to repay. Even if you sin and have labored at good deeds, goodness can heal your blemish, if you are discerning. Great was the wrongdoing of the firstborn, who committed sexual sin with his father’s wife, but because he had planned good in his heart, Moses showed him mercy. By a sentence of judgment his father cut him off from the inheritance, but through the loving intention he had formed, Moses healed him. He had been planning to rescue Joseph, and the one who examines everyone counted that intention as a deed. For grace seeks an opening from the repentant, and in its love mercifully forgives everything he owes. Reuben committed sexual sin and did a shameful thing in his father's bed, but because he conceived a good intention in his heart, his transgression was passed over. And if this intention received a fine reward, how great is the recompense for a good deed wherever it is done! Reuben also gave advice to his brothers, as we have said, that Joseph should be thrown into the pit without being killed. They listened to his words, although their envy had not died down, and they agreed with him that Joseph should be mistreated in the pit. Then they seized him as the crucifiers seized the Son of God, and stripped off his clothes just as they did to the Son in the courtroom. They mocked him as they mocked our Lord when he was being questioned. They taunted him, and he remained silent, just as Christ did not speak. One called him a dreamer of dreams with great mockery. Another held him to strip his tunic off him. One wanted them to throw him into a pit in a desolate place. Another, in great anger, threatened to kill him. One called him, “King of dreams, where is your crown?” They were all shouting from every side, while Joseph remained silent. That moment resembled the hour of our Lord's trial, when he was being insulted with every kind of outcry in the courtroom. It was a time when the sword was raised against the handsome young man, and he did not speak, so as not to mar the image of the Son. They also took Christ's clothes when he was being questioned, and great mockery was directed at him, as it was at Joseph. One was weaving a crown of thorns as though for a king. Another was preparing a garment of mockery to clothe him in. One was spitting in his face in contempt. Another covered him and asked him, “Who struck you?” Joseph had come to resemble this image when he was being taunted among his brothers whom he had visited. The shadow of the great killing fell upon that young man and confined him in the pit, to portray the tomb of the Son of God. Reuben said that they should not shed Joseph's blood, because he wanted to rescue him from their hands if he could. The judge, too, had intended to rescue our Lord, and when he could not, he washed his hands concerning his killing. Reuben and Pilate had the same desire: they did not want the blood of Joseph and of our Savior to be shed. Because Joseph portrayed the likeness of the Son of God, he portrayed in his own person the entire course of his great trial. Even the words that were heard from Pilate were not missing there, for they were being spoken by Reuben himself. “Let us not shed Joseph's blood,” Reuben said. The judge, too, absolved himself of the Son's blood. Joseph walked in the footsteps of the Son's trial and did not turn aside this way or that from his interrogations. He was bound to it throughout his journey like a shadow to a body, and his story encamped and traveled with him wherever he went. Who could look on while the servant and his Lord were being questioned and suppose that there was any difference between their interrogations? When envy was stirred up in the wilderness against the handsome young man, and the brothers' anger blazed against the wronged man, while they were oppressing him and insulting him with their words, and murderous fury was raging within them to put him to death, while they were taking his clothes from him without remorse and confining him in the pit, he did not speak. Through all these things, silence held him. He was wise enough not to distort the image of the sufferings he was honoring. He was insulted and would not open his mouth. He was mocked and maintained that silence of Christ. In this, my lord, the wronged Joseph resembled the Son. He did not speak, lest he become confused on the path he had taken. By remaining silent, he portrayed the one who was led like a lamb to slaughter. Like a ewe before its shearer, he did not speak. He was stripped of his tunic among his brothers, like the Son who stood naked on the cross. It was fitting for chaste Joseph, when he was exposed, to become an image of the exposure of the Son of God. He was stripped and innocent, and he was beaten without any fault, for in all his sufferings he was wholly an image of our Savior. O brothers, why this dishonor for Joseph? What cause brought upon him these sufferings that he endured? He brought provisions from his father; why is he being dishonored? He left his own country to visit the flock; why is he dying? He brought a greeting of peace; why is anger inflamed against him? His path is one of peace, and your anger is not his doing. He committed no wrong, and it is not just that he should be beaten. He resembles his Lord, and this is the cause that brought these things upon him. To the crucifiers, then, let us address that same cry: You murderers, why is the Son crucified? He brought the Father's peace to the world; why is he mocked? His compassion sent him to save Adam; why is he dying? Look, he carries healing for the sick; why these wounds? He is free from wrongdoing, so what is the reason for the sentence of death? This is the reality of that shadow, innocent Joseph, who portrayed in his own person everything that the Son of God endured. These are the heirs of those who are the heads of the tribes, and through envy they acquired one and the same evil will. No one ever inherited his father and acquired his treasures as the crucifiers inherited their fathers in every respect. No one ever mixed colors for a portrait and achieved such a likeness as Joseph did when he portrayed the Son without any difference. He fell into a pit in which there was no water, just as Joseph laid Christ in a new tomb in which there were no dead. A pit and a tomb, for the servant and his Lord, had been prepared. Neither water in the one nor dead bodies in the other were within their chambers. Mud and water did not wet Joseph in the pit, nor in the tomb did decay gain power over our Lord. Although the servant closely resembled his Lord in every aspect, the Lord's image is beyond all limits in its glories. Let Joseph remain a little distance from the Savior, so that the Only Son may travel his path alone. Like a mighty warrior, the freeborn Son entered Sheol, and as he came out, he emptied all the treasuries of death. He poured out hope upon the departed in their chambers, and he set milestones of peace in the place of destruction as he came out. He descended alone and ascended with many, as it is written. He uprooted Sheol and returned in strength to his Father's country. As far as this Joseph did not reach; let Joseph stand aside. Nor is he required to perform these mighty deeds. He is weaker than our Lord, as a shadow is weaker than a body. He sketched a likeness and made it as beautiful as he could. Envy crushed him, just as Christ was crucified through envy. His brothers hated him, just as the priests hated the Son of God. They stripped off his clothes, and this happened to our Savior. They mocked his dreams, and that same thing happened to the Only Son. They confined him in a pit, which also resembled the Son’s tomb. For this reason he bears an image of the sufferings, as I have said. I will now leave his story, which is full of beautiful things, for the account of him is long, and I am too weak for its greatness. Let my discourse rest on his great journey, wrapped in mysteries, for many mountains stand before it for it to cross with him. The discourse has drawn me as far as the pit and has given me rest. Blessed is the Son of the Living One, who was depicted in all the righteous.
The Third Discourse on Joseph
The Third Discourse on Joseph, When He Was Sold by His Brothers, by Saint Mar Jacob

The discourse has drawn me to walk along Joseph’s path. In you, my Lord, may my discourse rest, weary from accompanying the handsome one. Rachel’s firstborn has again called me to the pit to see him. Lord of Jacob, through you I will speak about his beloved. You are the treasury of all discourses about the truth, and from you my discourse receives strength to speak. Through you, Savior, I will see how beautiful Joseph is, for apart from you there is nothing that possesses beauty. The eye receives the sun’s radiance and clothes itself in light. From it the eye receives the ability to distinguish colors and forms. The eye cannot even see the sun itself except through the sun. It clothes the eye in radiance so that it can see both the sun and everything else. Nor does the mind possess light by its own nature; rather, it receives light from you to speak about your hidden nature. From you Joseph received radiance to make him beautiful. In you may the ugly one’s discourse be adorned, so that it may recount his beauties. See, discerning people, in what colors Joseph was portrayed: all his beauty shone with the Son’s pigments. Envy had thrown him into the pit and rested, having done its work, just as the Crucified One had entered the tomb and those who crucified him rested. Envy buried him alive in the pit as though he were dead, and clapped its hands to mock him, as it did our Lord. They had gathered to eat bread, Joseph’s brothers, as though at a celebration above a tomb containing a living man. And how many such things were being said by those spiteful men at that meal, which gave birth to murder in great fury! “Where are the dreams now, and their interpretations? If they are true, let them show the power of their revelations. Where is the light that used to bow down to this liar? Look, he is being cruelly mistreated in the darkness! Where are the sun and moon that bowed down to him? Let them send their rays to him, since they became his servants! Eleven stars used to bow down to him, as he claimed. Then let a single ray descend to him in the pit! Small is the dominion given him by the dreams he declared true: they have made him king inside a pit, in the darkness! Well suited to him is the cramped place where he is being battered, for pride deserves to be thrown into the depths. Where is that sheaf of his that stood upright, as he claimed? Let him now reap bitter sufferings from inside the pit! Where is that sleep of his that gave him leadership? Let him sleep now in the pit and see where he rules! The darkness of the pit that torments him is good for him, so that he will no longer go astray through deceptive visions.” They were mocking him like those who crucified the Son of God, who buried him and thought they had escaped his authority. And while that truthful man was being mocked by liars, and they were ridiculing him and thinking that he had departed and his story was finished, and while distress rose against Joseph in the darkness of the pit, and he was about to become entangled in the pangs of death in that place The wilderness. The mystery of the Son visited him in the pit and gave him a hand, to add beauty to him through the likeness of the Son of God. And while these things were being said to the handsome young man, so that Joseph would not be terrified by the darkness of the pit: “You have other milestones to pass along the Son’s road. The place of the pit does not mark your limit, where your journey will end. You must go to Egypt, Joseph, and prepare there a place for your Lord, for he too has set his face toward there. Go down; announce to the land that rebels against instruction that, look, the teacher who teaches the truth is coming to it. Go, tell the mistress of sorcery that there is arriving the one who by his power exposes all falsehood. Come up, Joseph! You will not die on the road on which you have been cast, for it is not yours to engage in battle with destruction. Set milestones on the road of blood, then pass on and leave, for your Lord is coming and will bring peace to it through his great slaughter. You will go to Egypt, for the Son’s road leads there, and on it is set the suffering of the slain King who subdues it. Go, tell that wandering land: ‘Coming to you is the great Shepherd, who has gone out to seek the lost.’ Come up from the pit and hasten your run with the good news, for the road is in haste, and a great slaughter is being carried in procession along it.” These mysteries visited the young man who was envied, in the pit, and directed the road into Egypt, as we have said. And when the divine plan was ready to carry out its work, the will of providence drew a caravan through the wilderness. Midianite merchants came and arrived there. Yes, they truly were merchants, in the fullest sense! Their trade and their good name were fitting for them, for they brought down a great treasure to Egypt, which was in need: a choice pearl, great and worthy in its value. They were being urged, as though under compulsion, to come forward and buy. And while the affair was being directed by God, Judah was giving his brothers advice about the matter. “What do we gain by killing our brother?” he was saying to them. “Come,” he said, “let us sell him, and let our hand not be against him.” For it was fitting for Judah to give this advice, since the company of twelve, all his brothers, is associated with his name. The twelve tribes are stamped with his name, and it was fitting for him to take part in the course of the mysteries of the truth. The designation of his name embraces all the tribes of Jacob, for the great Savior was to descend through his tribe. It was fitting for this man to take part willingly in Joseph’s journey, which had been marked out by the Most High. “Come,” he said, “let us sell him, and let our hand not be against him.” They heard these words and prepared to carry out the deed. And for this reason, Judah, your brothers will praise you, because through your advice they did not plunge into the blood of that innocent man. “Come,” he said, “let us sell him,” and they all listened to his good advice. They pulled him up out of the pit so that he could be sold. And while God was sending him to Egypt to provide relief, Judah began what had been commanded by God. He was sent down to provide abundance for the hungry, and even if they had been unwilling, he would not have been held back from his journey. For he was sent ahead of them, as it is written, while their evil will was serving his own purpose. The sons of slave women became masters over the son of the free woman, and as though he were a slave, they shamelessly sold him for a price. The freeborn man was silent as he was sold and did not complain, for he was resembling that Lord who became a slave. He enters He took on the yoke of slaves and did not protest, for the mystery of the Son brought him into subjection. He submitted to slavery while his freedom remained intact within him. It was like the Son, who became a slave while remaining free. He was silent as he was sold, and they took his price, while he accepted it, so that everything belonging to the Son might be seen in him throughout his whole journey. He bowed his head as a new slave, full of freedom, and entered slavery to serve, although he was free. He resembled the Lord of the nations, who became a slave, while his lordship remained hidden within him as he submitted to slavery. The Arabs bought Joseph as a slave, although he was a free man. The Hebrews sold Jesus to die, although he gives life to the dead. Judah handed Joseph over for sale to the Midianites, and here Judas was likewise taking the price of our Lord. The free man went down, became a slave, and bought Egypt. This is the likeness of the Son, who redeemed creation through his humiliation. Joseph completed the Son’s journey and then began it again. Let us go back and bring forward what I left behind in the mountains already passed. He came up from the pit as from a grave, unharmed, and again began to portray the sufferings of the crucifixion. They buried him in the pit, and he came up without corruption, like our Lord. Then, once again, from the beginning of the road, he began to walk along it. The free man entered slavery, as you have heard, because he had not yet applied this color to the image he had portrayed. Little by little he completed the picture of the realities, gathering from every side the beautiful features that suited him. It was fitting for him to be sold by his brothers, just as Christ was sold by his disciple. It was fitting for him to set his face toward Egypt, to go down and increase the supply of food for the hungry within the land. He submitted to slavery and took on the yoke of subjection, and set out to travel with merchants along the road he had taken. The mystery sent a message to Egypt through him as he traveled: “Prepare a place for the Lord of slaves, for he is coming to you. I have sent Joseph to make preparations before him. Learn from him what treasures are hidden in the King who is coming to you. Look at the slave and learn from him about his Lord: what riches he will distribute in the land when he comes down to it. See how wise the administration of the young man I have sent is, and learn from this that the Ancient of Days is beyond all limits. Look at this man who distributes food to the hungry among you, and be assured through him that the one coming to you is a treasury of life. I am sending you a taste of the Lord through Joseph the slave. Learn from him that the Lord is entirely nourishment for those who hunger for him. Take from the son of Jacob a likeness of the Son of God, for it is he who distributes food to the hungry throughout the lands.” The mystery secretly sent this good news through Joseph to Egypt, to which he went down with the merchants. Although he was free, he took on slavery and traveled on his way. Yet his brothers’ hatred did not leave him alone. They slaughtered a young goat and stained his tunic with its blood, so that even far away he would be slain at their hands. Envy sold him and was not satisfied that he had moved elsewhere. And again his tunic was being dyed with blood because of it. Joseph was traveling along the road to Egypt with the merchants, while his brothers’ wrath crouched over his tunic. They called it to account in Joseph’s place, which it had occupied, for in their hatred they dyed it with blood as though it were a corpse. The great mystery of the crucifixion overflowed to them. And without knowing it, they completed the pattern of the realities. That tunic was the one on which the mysteries had been depicted, and blood alone was missing from its images. If it had not been dyed with blood, as a symbol, it would not have been completed in the colors of the crucifixion. If a sword had not been drawn against the tunic, its color would have been dull compared with that of the cross, although it was its symbol. All the beauty of the crucifixion was the blood that came down upon it. And where the outpouring of blood is missing, there is no cross. It was fitting for the splendid image that Jacob had drawn to be completed in the color of blood, which is beautiful. He made [?] and established the design of the crucifixion. Blood alone was holding back its completion, and now it was completed. He had fashioned a cross but had not put all its impressions upon it. The splashed color was missing from it, and then it was completed. But when he looked into the mystery and saw what it needed, he dipped the stamps in blood and arranged their impressions upon it to make it beautiful. The cross was truly depicted on that tunic, and it was not completed except through the blood in which it was dyed. This image had been missing from this garment, and when it was placed upon it, it was completed in all its beauty. See how many mysteries Joseph bore upon his splendor—in his own person, in his tunic, and in his deeds! For if these beauties had not been woven into him, he would not have shone with all this preeminence. “He placed his testimony in Joseph”: understand from this that he had been appointed in every way to be a witness to the Son. i. Not even the boy’s clothing was ordinary among his brothers. He was honored with a tunic unlike the usual kind. His clothing itself was clothed in symbols of the realities, so that Joseph might be an image of the Son in every part of his being. Joseph’s brothers slaughtered a young goat over the tunic and dyed it with blood, and the great image was completed upon it. The crucifiers hung the Son of God upon the wood, and the shameful cross was spattered with his holy blood. In wine he dyed his clothing, and in the blood of grapes his covering. His pattern was in Joseph, whose tunic they dyed with blood. That tunic had been dyed as a symbol, and they sent it to Jacob so that the old man might see his son’s murder. “We found this. Take it and see whether it belongs to your son.” A great deception, carried out with a skill full of murder! Envy had entered the chosen company whom Jacob fathered, and it corrupted the order of truth that was there. From it sprang murder, deceit, and falsehood, for it is like a root with bitter branches. It yoked a freeborn man under the yoke of slaves and felt no sorrow. It also prepared to lie, and still it was not satisfied. It brought the old man news of murder and had no pity on him as he grieved bitterly over his beloved. Envy threw these good arrangements into confusion, so that the brothers hated their father, their brother, and God. They sold their brother, deceived their father, and despised God. They enslaved Joseph, mocked Jacob, and sinned against the Lord. They had no pity on the freeborn man who became a slave. On the old man who was steeped in mourning they had no compassion. They gave no thought to the Lord who saw their deeds. In everything they disregarded duty and rebuke. Joseph was enslaved, Jacob was mourning, and the Lord was angry. Because the brothers were full of envy, they neglected everything. Little by little Evil enters those who practice it, takes hold [?] throughout the soul, and is absorbed into it. It needs only a little room to invade free will. i. Once it has taken a small place for itself, it conquers the territory. Joseph’s brothers at first only envied him, but when envy grew in its place, it produced [?]. Its tree grew strong enough to yield the fruits of death, and it enslaved them to many evils. Who could look at the old man who was grieving bitterly as though for someone dead, and not reveal to him that Joseph was alive? Who could sell his brother, though he was freeborn, and all the gates of his compassion shut on every side? Who could despise God like this while knowing him, and commit all this wickedness as they did? Envy grew and nurtured the evil of their thoughts, until it became strong enough for the soul itself to be engulfed in it. “Here is a tunic. Take it and see whether it is your son’s.” Jacob saw it and tore his cloak in great sorrow. The old man was shaken, and anguish seized him over his beloved. “Yes, it is Joseph’s tunic, and my son has been killed! A vicious animal must have torn him apart in a deserted place. Joseph, my beloved son, has been killed! What can I do for him?” Yes, truly, a vicious animal had seized him: his brothers’ fury, which was fiercer than lions. A beast thirsting for blood and murder rushed upon the boy: resentment, which in its bitterness is worse than a viper. Envy attacked him, beside which a lion is nothing. It bore down upon him in a deserted place, and no one rescued him. Jacob’s words about his beloved were true: a vicious animal had attacked him—his brothers’ hatred. He saw his son’s corpse in the tunic that had been given to him, and he fell upon it, grieving bitterly as over someone dead. He embraced it and wailed, crying out in great sorrow, and he kissed the blood upon it as though he were kissing Joseph. “In mourning I will go down to my son in the abode of the dead, for the pain of the boy’s murder is too great for consolation.” And why indeed was this mystery hidden, and why did the Lord not reveal to his friend Jacob what had happened to Joseph? He was a man who had prevailed and bound the angel in his zeal, and in the revelations at Bethel he was rich. Come, listen to him as he called his sons to show them what would happen to them all from God in the last days. He excluded one from the number of the twelve, and he divided two among the tribes and scattered them. He looked ahead at the chosen tribe of the fourth son and revealed to his sons that the great Savior would arise from it. He disclosed to each of his sons what would happen to him. How, then, was this mystery hidden from him here? He described future events and how they would happen, yet it is astonishing that he did not know what was about to happen. He revealed concerning our Lord that he would wash his clothing in wine, yet he did not recognize that the kid’s blood was not his son’s. He understood distant things as though they were near, while nearby things were hidden from him, and he did not know them. The things he knew through revelation were put to use, while those he did not know were concealed for a purpose. In Isaac himself, too, we see something like this again: there were times when he was deprived of knowledge. He held Jacob and blessed him as though he were Esau, and although he knew that his words would stand, he did not know this. Providence concealed their meaning from him for the sake of the arrangements for the future events that were to take place. [?] were. There the younger Jacob filled the place of the firstborn, and for this reason the Lord did not reveal that it was Jacob. Here the Lord sent Joseph to prepare the way. If he had revealed it to Jacob his father, he would have held him back. Where necessary, revelations shone forth; and when it was not necessary, they were concealed from understanding. The mystery of the Son was the treasurer for all the righteous, and it wisely administered their revelations. It stole Joseph away from Jacob, who was holding fast to him. For if he had known, he would not have let him undertake his journey. Until he had completed the journey for which he went down, he did not reveal it to his father, lest he prevent him from carrying out his task. Along with this, it happened for another purpose: when his father became convinced that Joseph had been killed and grieved, he portrayed an image of the great mourning for the Only Son. He depicted the entrance in his cloak when he tore it. Through the killing of his son, his father was portraying the front of the entrance. It was fitting for the aged Jacob to do this. He saw the tunic stained with blood and tore his garments, for he had been stirred by the great image of the crucifixion. He put on sackcloth to portray there also the darkness that the Father spread over creation at the killing of his Son. He honored the suffering because of the killing of the son of his old age. Through the garment he tore and the sackcloth in which he clothed himself, he was imitating, my Lord, the fatherhood of the Father, who, though he does not suffer, adopted the appearance of mourning. He tore the entrance of the sanctuary over his beloved, and spread darkness over the regions and made them gloomy. Through the mourning he performed, he showed the tenderness of fatherhood, and solemnly marked the killing of his Only Son throughout the whole world. Jacob took on a great likeness when he grieved, so that he might solemnly mark that suffering of the Son in a mystery. That tunic stained with blood was spread out, and the cross bearing sufferings stood before the righteous man. It was stretched out with its sleeves and the blood upon it, and the crucifixion was clearly seen in it. Jacob himself also offered gifts that were fitting for him: his cloak, which he tore, and the sackcloth he put on in grief. Jacob's house became Golgotha in a mystery when that tunic stained with blood entered it. The old man mourned and wore sackcloth over his beloved, and portrayed the darkness that covered the earth at the killing of the Son. The cloak was torn in that same likeness of which we have spoken, for Israel too was a sanctuary of the Godhead. There was great mourning in Jacob's house because of Joseph, just as there was mourning in the world over the killing of the Son of God. The whole world clothed itself in black because of our Lord, and in the darkness that covered the earth everything was [?]. The sanctuary curtain tore itself in bitterness, so that the great death of the Only Son would not pass as something ordinary. Jacob made his whole household grieve because of Joseph. His sons and daughters were comforting him, but he would not cease. The Father shook the whole world at the killing of his Son, to confirm to created beings through the shaking that he is the Only Son. This likeness stole the mystery away from the righteous man, so that he would not know where Joseph was when he was sold. He did not know, so that he might solemnly mark the suffering of the Son. For if he had known, he would not have grieved or solemnly marked it. It was therefore fitting that he grieved, so that the suffering of the Son might be honored. Blessed is he who through his suffering revealed the hidden things that had been concealed.
The Fourth Homily on Joseph
The fourth homily on Joseph by Saint Mar Jacob: when he was wronged by his mistress.

The account of the chaste man has given me material through its reading, and I cannot help sailing on the sea of his beauties. The young Joseph, who won victory through his purity, again asks me to raise my voice in songs about him. That freeborn man who became a slave among the Egyptians has invited speech to recount his beauties wherever he was. The apostle who went down to depict the mystery of apostleship has filled me with wonder as I speak of his victories. The Lord sent him to prepare the way before his descent, and he became a witness to the proclamation of true things. The power of the mystery accompanied him on the road he took, and he spoke in a new language without having learned it. It had fallen to his lot to go down into Egypt; when he went down, he heard a language he did not know. He went out to trace that great road of the apostles: To speak in a new language in foreign lands. For it is written that he heard a language he did not know, Because the whole course of apostleship was depicted in him. In these righteous people, leaven was preserved for the whole world, And he scattered them throughout the lands to make them fragrant. He called Abraham from his father's household to the land of Canaan, And the boy Isaac away from his mother to become a sacrifice. He sent Jacob fleeing on the road to Haran, and he left his country. And Joseph's lot was the land of Egypt, where he would be sold. Like salt, he scattered them throughout the lands, So that through that flavor the way that had been tasteless might acquire flavor. Through them he was depicting this course of apostleship, by which he sent light to the whole world through the disciples. Through these mysteries the image of the Son shone upon the regions, and they received its light in one form after another. Joseph, then, went down with the merchants as one who had been sent, and he reached Egypt with providence accompanying him. He was to go down and teach holiness to the lover of adultery, so that the whole country might adopt his chaste ways. This was the work assigned to him among the Egyptians: to become a mirror for the country, so that it might adorn itself through him. One warrior from that lineage of Abraham's household went down to give flavor to the elders of contemptible Ham. The pure boy was sent by righteousness to impart wisdom to the elders through his vigilance. He was sent to the land of slaves to rebuke them, showing that slavery is not natural to human beings. He was a slave, yet conducted himself chastely, to rebuke Ham, who had degraded himself by his own choice. Let anyone to whom the lot of slaves has fallen look at Joseph, who was able to love both God and his masters. Time carried him away and yoked him under the yoke of subjection, and without abandoning God, he performed a slave's work. He honored his masters and did not distance himself from God. He became a slave, yet conducted himself as a free man. With virtue he guarded what God's household had entrusted to him, and through diligence he showed his love for his masters. Come closer and see him being handed over to merchants, yet remaining unchanged in his freedom wherever he went. The Midianites received his price from the Egyptians, but because he knew that the Lord was with him, he was not grieved. He traveled with the merchants, subject to them throughout his journey. In Egypt he was sold again, and he accepted it. His masters changed from place to place, but he did not exchange the freedom that came from God. He entered an Egyptian household to work without discouragement. His heart was sincere, he was attentive to his work, and he loved his masters. He devoted himself to serving a temporary master whose time would run its course, while his love was bound to that lordship which takes no orders. He was wise and knew how to see clearly. He sincerely honored both the Lord and his masters. The young man was discerning enough to distinguish and give each his due: glory to the Lord, and to his masters the labor of his brothers. He kept himself pure for God, without disgrace, and worked diligently in submission to the Egyptians. Before God he was pure and clear, fair and spotless; before his master he was diligent and ready, devoted and constant. He loved the Lord and did not despise his master either. One good will served both sides. Time yoked him to the yoke of slaves, and he proved diligent under it. Under that same yoke he served both God and his masters. When he was freeborn, he gave his father comfort and increased his love. When he became a slave, he amazed his master with his goodness. But both in slavery and in freedom, he truly loved God, cherished him, and honored him. The Lord blessed the work of his hands among the Egyptians so that he would be loved, and he managed affairs wisely. Help accompanied his deeds. The Lord granted success through his hands, so that he might accomplish every good thing. His master's household was blessed because of him. Whatever he did prospered and increased in his hands. He was righteous and upright, and diligent in his master's household. Everything he did was directed by grace. If he undertook work in the house, it prospered; and if he went out to the field, the crops increased. The Egyptian's household was blessed because of Joseph—everything he owned, both in the house and in the field. The image of the Son cast its shadow among the Egyptians, and it supported his deeds with blessings. He entered the banquet and gave wine to those who needed it. He went out into the wilderness and multiplied bread for those who were hungry. From that reality a shadow had come into being in the Egyptian's household, and it blessed that household through Joseph's hands. Joseph bore the Son’s disgrace when he was sold, and through him he prospered and became victorious in his deeds. He resembled his Lord, and both in the house and in the wilderness everything flourished through his divine care. As he relied on that great image of the Son, the household of his masters benefited from his blessings. Whatever he did prospered abundantly, and through his hands good things increased for everyone around him. The household grew strong through his wise management, and everywhere the work of his hands was blessed. While he resembled the Son in his beauty and splendor, sin grew jealous and sought to throw mud on the beautiful one. His mistress saw the handsome young man and was dying of desire to corrupt the young man’s beloved chastity. Look how much of Christ’s beauty there is in Joseph: he too stood firm in the struggle, like Christ, and did not weaken. Sin gazed at our Lord as the Egyptian woman gazed at Joseph, and clung to him for a long time in unceasing combat. She set a snare for him to test his strength and see whether he could be tripped up. She hid her traps, but he cut through them all and passed beyond them. She arrayed before him all the enticements of desirable things. But with his determination he scorned deceit in all its forms. Through fasting he exposed the love of food and escaped it, and through his humility, the love of glory and power. In every contest sin was defeated by the Savior. It was fitting that Joseph should conquer, since he was his likeness. The Egyptian woman too sought an opportunity against the desirable young man. She drew up a battle line of lust to fight against the beautiful one. But the young man had armed himself with holiness so that he would not corrupt the beauty of the image he honored. He saw the shameless woman arraying her beauty to fight against him, and with chastity he established a battle line that would not give way. He kept himself holy behind the solid barrier of holiness, opposing and striking down the surge of hateful lust. It was fitting for him to conquer in the struggle of youth, so that he would not distort the likeness of the struggle of the one who conquers all. It is fitting for this discourse to recount his beauties at length, for the image he left among the scriptural readings is greatly beloved. His story is chaste, and the account of him rests on purity. It is entirely beautiful to anyone who looks with clear understanding. He conquered in the battle in which all mighty men are brought low, and faced the ordeal in which even the diligent falter. He conquered the one who conquered Samson, who had conquered and killed the lion, and who drowned the mighty sons of the judges in the waters. Adam, the ancestor of the human race, had fallen into this snare, but Joseph trampled it, broke it, and escaped from it. A great net had been spread for the nimble young man, but he tore it and passed through; despite its breadth, it did not trip him up. Even the angels watched Joseph’s battle: in the asp’s own hole he brought it low by his steadfastness. In the leopard’s den he fought with a lioness, and he was not defeated by her, for the chaste man who faced her was courageous. See, you discerning people, how wonderful was that champion’s battle: how, and how greatly, and in what manner he conquered through his diligence. In his youth, the realm of passions and unrestrained impulses, his battle continually changed from day to day; Inside a bedroom that lent itself to secret deeds, and in slavery, whose way of life is lax about what is right; While desire set his nature ablaze with its heat, and the woman enticing him was the mistress to whom he was subject; And inside her own house she sought her opportunity with a member of her household, and the battle made it easy for the young man to fall—yet he did not fall. In this fierce place Joseph fought, and nothing at all could weaken his steadfastness. His mistress commanded, but he did not obey her, though he bowed before her. Desire blazed, but he was not burned by it, though he stood within it. The deed was easy, but he did not approach it, though it was within his reach. Their contact was constant, but every day he rejected her. Constant contact is far worse than the stirrings of foul desire, for through persistence even flint can be melted. A person can overcome an ugly encounter that confronts him head-on, and if a battle unexpectedly assails him, he can prevail over it. But whoever overcomes constant contact—his battle is wonderful. He resembles Joseph, who overcame its persistence and was crowned. Within the mind there is a hidden battle every day, and in thought a person either conquers or is condemned. Sometimes even a weak mind conquers, but because it is deprived of contact, this is no victory. And after a time, if it meets a feeble attack, that attack dies down, and the person escapes injury. Pure Joseph did not conquer in this way, through favorable circumstances; rather, his victory was genuine and full of wonder. While his daily contact with his mistress enticed him, a single, unchanging resolve remained within him. Though the battle turned against him every day, there was never a time when Joseph fell away from victory. The snare ran alongside his feet wherever he went, yet even when he stepped on it, he did not fall, because he was shrewd. The mistress enticed the slave, but he would not consent.
