Although he utterly rejected all her words, he did not treat her with contempt. He gently admonished her, without contempt, so that she would know in what matters it was right for him to obey her. And these were the sorts of things the wise man said to his mistress every day when she threatened him with harm: “I have never forgotten that I am your slave, nor do I forget it now. My mind acknowledges that you are my mistress, bows before you, and submits to you. “It is also laid upon me to obey your command every day; but I cannot do this thing that I have heard from you.” In matters that are proper, I honor you as my mistress; but as for improper things, I beg you, let them pass. Apart from this, I obey you in whatever you ask of me. Nor would I resist you in this, if it were right. It is not right for me to be treacherous and hate my master, and to forfeit my life with God through this wickedness. Perhaps that shameless woman said to chaste Joseph, “Why have you rejected my words, though they deserve respect? It is no disgrace for you to do my will, son of the Hebrews. I am the one who would descend from freedom to become your slave. It is an honor for you to do what I tell you. I am the one who has lowered myself by coming to your door in need. I am the one who has stepped down a rank from my high position. But you, young man, are not brought low by the deed. Fortune has turned against me, so that I must ask you to do my will. But your own rank will raise you up when you obey me. I am the one who has fallen from the high position I held. But you, young man, stand to rise if you obey me.” Joseph said, “I will not fall away from God, nor will I put a stain on your status as a free woman. Rather, by my chastity and upright conduct I protect you, so that the order of what is good may not be overturned by my hands. Why should you fall away from the love of marriage and cast me, too, out of fellowship with God? Remain a free woman who keeps faith with her husband, and let me remain a slave who has not sinned against the Lord in his masters’ house. It is good for you to remain faithful to your husband, and my part, in turn, is to keep the trust I have with God. Why bring shame on yourself by betraying your husband, and sin on me by my overstepping my duty? Remain free and in authority without harm, and let me remain in peace and in slavery without sin. Do not join the ranks of adulteresses, nor let me become one of the sexually immoral because of you. See, I am preserving my chastity and your status as a free woman. That is why I will not do what you have asked of me.” The immoral woman said, “You ought to follow my will, because I am your mistress, and if you do not obey, it is rebellion. I have seen your faithfulness, and you have shown your good judgment well. But as for what I desire, you can no longer resist me. If obeying me is blameworthy, the blame rests with me. And if it is a sin, it is entirely mine, and you are far removed from it. I have compelled you, and there is no way for you not to answer me. You ought to obey what I have told you, since it pleases me. What mistress gives orders in her house and is not obeyed? Or what slave does not submit to his master’s wife? See that you do not forget a slave’s place in your arrogance, and despise my words because I have stooped to speak to you.” Joseph said, “I have another Master who is unseen. Without denying your authority, I serve him.” “By what deed have I disregarded your word, or do I disregard it now? Only in this matter, because it would be a great wickedness for both me and you.” “When have I disobeyed the command of your ladyship? Only in this matter, because I stand in dread of God.” “That hidden Master of mine greatly loves chastity, and if I fall into the snare of adultery, he becomes angry.” “There is a limit to how far I must submit to you, and I also know how I must serve that Master.” “In everything required of servants, I honor you; and whatever the fear of the Lord requires, I observe.” “This has been the custom of our people from ancient times: that no one commit sexual sin with his neighbor’s wife or with another woman.” “How could I violate the rule of my ancestors’ household, sin against the Lord, and join myself to my master’s wife in adultery?” A relentless battle was drawn up every day against the pure man, and every day he proved himself a warrior through unfailing victory. The battle remained awake against the valiant man all his days; he could not take off the armor of his courage. He could neither avoid the struggle nor flee from it. The battle was within the house, and he belonged to the household—what could he do? The woman who stirred up battle every day was the mistress of the house, while he was a servant within the house, working even as he fought. Should he prepare for battle or apply himself diligently to his work? Should he obey his mistress or gain purity? A tumultuous battle pressed upon him from every side, but he drove back the forces of the conflict and was not defeated. Day after day he escaped harm, and little by little he put on a crown filled with victories. With a single, pure, steadfast purpose that did not change, he remained watchful every day, and therefore he was not defeated as he fought. He was not defeated at one time and victorious at another, for he did not grow slack and surrender to defeat. Sin was exceedingly hateful in his eyes when it was practiced, and he struggled not to commit wrongdoing in secret. Listen as he says to his master’s wife, “How could I do this great evil and sin against the Lord?” He called the sin he hated “a great evil”: “How,” he said, “could I do this great evil?” Sin is difficult for someone who loves righteousness; he is virtually unable to practice wrongdoing because he hates it. In someone whose will is truly awake to good things, the thought inclined toward evil lies asleep. “How,” he said, “could I do this great evil?” It was as though someone were saying, “It cannot be done, because it is so very great.” He looked at sin, and it seemed to him like a great pit; the young man resolved that there was no possibility of his going down into it. He looked upon wrongdoing as a [?] full of terror, and shrank back from it, so that he would not peer into it and begin to tremble. He saw sin and compared it to a pit of snakes, and the pure man declared that if he went down into it, he would not come back up. He saw that it was a great evil, and therefore said, “How could I do this and sin against the Lord?” Wrongdoing does not seem great to someone who practices it every day, nor does sin seem hateful to the person who keeps committing it. Sin is commonplace and insignificant to the person who commits it, and therefore he does not even tremble at his own deed. When the soul becomes accustomed to evil, it is dyed with it and takes on its color, and no longer sees how ugly it is. Someone whose eye is pure and hates wrongdoing can see how very ugly it is, and hates it too. Joseph looked a little way ahead with clear sight. He saw that sin was a great evil, and fled. He saw the trap and turned aside from it while he was still far away, so that he would not become entangled among the snares laid for him. He saw that sin was a great evil and said, “How could I do this and sin against the Lord?” Because he had seen that it was a great evil, he escaped from it; for even a hunted animal that sees a trap does not fall into it. It was fitting for this man to bear the image of the Son, whom he honored through his purity in the land he had reached. Sin had been defeated by him, as it was by our Lord, and he emerged victorious from the contest without being stained. Although every day his foot stood firm in victory, every day the Egyptian woman renewed her struggle against him. Satan did not flee from our Lord at the first contest, nor did he withdraw from him at the second, when he was defeated. Sin lost in both the first and the second, and only when it was defeated in the third did it flee. Likewise, the Egyptian woman lost to the Hebrew every day, yet returned again to renew the struggle. She saw the pure man inside the chamber, and entered, panting, to fight him in that struggle she entered every day. She disgraced all womankind through her rashness, for the force of her desire carried her beyond what was proper. Not even nature shamed her into remaining calm, nor did she remain among those sinful women who do not act so rashly. She shamelessly seized the young man inside the room, to destroy the seal of his chastity with ease. Loathsome desire had burst over the wretched woman, but chaste Joseph would not drown in its foul sea. The lioness rushed to break the calf and make him her prey, but he escaped from her grasp unharmed. The she-wolf caught the lamb in her jaws to eat his flesh, but he left his wool behind, preserved his body, scorned her, and went out. Be spectators of this struggle, you listeners, for even the angels and all the demons marveled at it. He filled both the right and the left with amazement at how he scorned loathsome desire on its own ground. Here the beauty of the account of that beautiful man has overwhelmed us, and I cannot reach the end of his wondrous beauties. Leave him, O discourse, in the chamber as he struggles, and prepare a crown of praises to offer him. Here, then, is the discourse’s promise to its listeners: Joseph’s struggle will again be recounted at length. I will be silent now, and speak again about his victories. Through you, my Lord, may the ugly man who proclaims the beautiful man become beautiful. The fourth discourse on Joseph is ended.
The fifth discourse on Joseph.
The fifth discourse on Joseph: when his mistress slandered him and he was thrown into prison.

Ugly lust came down to battle with chastity. Come, let us contemplate that victory full of wonder. Pure Joseph stood in the arena against the Egyptian woman. Be spectators, and give praise to the victor. His story, as it was being told, had proceeded this far, and the discourse faltered while he, in the struggle, was showing his courage. The discourse left him fighting in the inner chamber. Let us now tell how he comes out victorious, for wondrous is the image that Joseph painted of purity. Let us learn and see with what colors he poured beauty into it, by what strength he banished lust from his limbs, and what enabled him to stand victorious. This must be made clear, so that we may know the means by which, and how, the passion of lust was extinguished in Joseph. The young man was abundantly filled with love for the Lord, and he left no room for anything else to dwell in him. Upon the image of the Godhead his gaze was fixed, and he did not turn his sight away from it, lest he become confused. In his wisdom he gave no opportunity for an ugly occurrence to stand between him and the Majesty and turn him away from it. The encounters of the world did not obscure his vision of it, so that sin would not enter secretly without his noticing it. The young man possessed an eye that discerned clearly, so that he could see wickedness while it was still far away and flee from it. He fixed his whole vision above so that it would be enlightened, and it watched closely lest sin be lurking somewhere. Every day he was alert at his watch, keeping an eye on himself; and whenever he heard the commotion of wickedness, he put on armor. He had made himself his own lookout, for he was wise, lest an ambush against his freedom be lurking on any side. Once he had shut the door of his soul against evil things, he opened it to the world and went in and out of it unharmed. And so, when sin knocked at him to enter, the bars were in place and weapons were arrayed above his gates. All his treasures were stored within chastity, and there were affixed seals of holiness upon all his gates. Whoever opens the doors of his soul to evil things finds it difficult to keep wickedness from entering it. And so, when passion enters through an open door, how long will you struggle against it, O soul, and where will you defeat it? Unless the soul is surrounded by a wall of vigilance, it is breached everywhere, and evil passions trample it. If it does not see ugly wickedness while it is still outside, when it enters, the soul is dyed with its sweetness. If it does not discern from afar the trap that has been set, once it falls into it, only with toil and difficulty does it escape from it. Whoever lifts his gaze and looks clearly escapes harm without toil. While passion is still far from him, he recognizes it. He puts on armor, goes out to meet it, and quenches it. Watchful Joseph therefore escaped harm: while sin was still far from him, he saw it and fled. He spotted the wrongdoing that had come out from its place to attack him. He went inside and left the evil outside the door. If from a distance you see sin and flee from it, it is too weak to come to your door once you have seen it. But if you lower your gaze from it while it enters you, it takes hold of [?] and tramples you in its insolence. In its own territory sin has mighty strength, and once it seizes the soul, the soul is ruined, while sin does not flee. The watchful soul shuts its doors so that it cannot enter, and sits quietly, undisturbed by the stranger. Joseph was serene and at peace away from evil things. For this reason he saw the evil and withdrew from it. The smell of wrongdoing struck him from a distance, and he began to flee, so that his pure self would not come into contact with that defilement. He had a sensitive sense of smell that knew how to distinguish, so that wherever there was the smell of wrongdoing he would flee from it. The smell of death reached him from the Egyptian woman, and because the smell had clung to his clothes, he let them go. He accepted that he would go out naked from the bedchamber rather than be stifled by the smell of wrongdoing inside the room. His pure sense of smell could not endure that smoke from the illicit fire that had come out to burn what did not belong to it. This is a mighty contest for anyone who watches it: youth overcoming lust inside the room. An ambush surrounded that champion inside the bedchamber, but because he was prepared, he did not surrender to guilt. A tumultuous struggle overtook him in a confined place without warning, but because he was ready beforehand, he overcame the danger of falling. Come near, listeners, and see a contest full of wonder: a young man fighting against a woman inside the room; a mistress seeking an opportunity with her slave, while he gives her no answer; a boy who scorns his master's wife and does not look at her. Hateful lust was being despised by youth, while holiness had taken possession of his young life. The boy was confined in [?] with a lioness, but because he was courageous, he overcame her in her own territory and escaped her. The lustful Egyptian woman attacked him inside her bedchamber, but because he was prepared to guard his treasure, he did not give way. In a place hidden from onlookers, he saw God, and he feared to commit wrongdoing in secret, for God was watching him. Inside the closed doors he perceived the one who examines everything, who looks intently at both hidden and visible things. He would not sow thorns in secret, because he knew that a time would come when the evil seed would be exposed. He would not accept that closed barriers could conceal his wrongdoing, because he understood that the one who sees everything is both inside and outside. His sight did not deceive the boy, for he was wise, so that he would sin in secret and scorn the Hidden One through wrongdoing. The young woman seized him in the darkness to have intercourse with him, but he fled to the open light that he loved. In concealment sin has the strength to carry out its work, and for this reason that discerning man fled into the street. She seized his clothes, but because he knew which vessel was precious, he held on to himself and let go of his clothing, which was nothing. He was exposed, but exposure meant nothing to him, for his modesty was not a matter of outward appearance intended to please people. He was bound to God. He loves true purity, not the outward appearance someone may acquire. Joseph was chaste and let go of his clothing because he was chaste, for it was of no account— the garment he left behind with foolishness. The young man was shrewd and understood like a wise man that everything he possessed outside himself was not truly his. To that possession of the soul he held fast, so that he would not be stripped of it. He gave the Egyptian woman his clothing so that he would not be hindered. She had wanted one thing, but she took something else instead. The young man defied her; the garment mocked her for how low she had sunk. Joseph's struggle was completed with an athlete's prowess, and he emerged victorious from the contest through his diligence. When he had escaped one struggle, he faced another: the struggle of injustice, which opened its mouth against the righteous man. Turbulent waves threatened him with their changing movements, but because he knew how to grapple with them, he did not sink. Envy assailed him, and he brought it into submission. And from his service with God he was not held back. The woman loved him and sought to corrupt his chastity, but because he was chaste, he triumphed in the contest of holiness. And when this fierce struggle was completed, injustice arose to do its work with a loud voice. Joseph's mistress saw from what had happened that she had been scorned, and she opened her mouth with lies against the wronged man. Desire turned into murderous rage, and hatred took the place of love to act through it. The same wickedness worked in her in another form. Whether she loved or hated, her deed was murder. She saw that she had been defeated and raised her voice and wept over Joseph, saying, “He came in to me to make a mockery of me!” She accused the innocent man, who was full of chastity, until the young man's master arrived, and she went out to meet him. She filled her mouth with lies against the wronged man and began to tell how careful she was and how she would not be led into wrongdoing. “Why,” she said, “a Hebrew slave to serve us? If I had answered him, he would have driven a wedge between you and me. The young man is corrupt, and he was deceiving us with his chastity. Every day he sought an opportunity to make a mockery of us. The young man rose up against me to act shamelessly in his corruption, and I raised my voice, and he let go of his clothing and went out and fled. Why should this man who despises his masters be your slave? If I had answered him, he was planning to seize your place. If I had not been very guarded and careful, our love would certainly have been corrupted by him. If I had not remained faithful in the absence of my husband, the slave you bought would have separated me from you to commit adultery with me. If I were a woman who loved adultery and hated her husband, this hater of his masters would have brought disgrace upon us. If my nobility had not surpassed that of other freeborn women, this man would have brought a sword into our house, as he intended. Why should we buy a bad reputation with money? Drive out the corrupt man who wanted to dishonor a freeborn woman in her own house! Unless he goes out, I will not come inside your door. I cannot bear to see before me a despicable man!” Great wickedness was being spoken aloud, injustice practiced with boundless skill. The handsome man was wronged, and the wronged man remained silent and did not speak. But the scorned woman raised her voice fiercely in defiance. Truth was concealed from those who saw and heard, and the truth was hidden, while falsehood showed its face openly. Justice was obstructed, and there was no room for uprightness. The innocent man was condemned, and guilt raised its head. It was also fitting that Joseph should be condemned while innocent, so that even in this he would not be unlike the image of the Son. It was fitting for him to be wronged while he was upright, so that he would not fall short of that beauty of the Son of God. The assembly contended against the upright one like the Egyptian woman. By the people's judgment the righteous one was judged through falsehood. The daughter of Shem the great became like the daughter of that contemptible Ham, and learned from her to lie against the Savior. The Hebrew woman cried out like the Egyptian woman, “He deserves death!” Our Lord remained silent like Joseph when he was questioned. Zion contended deceitfully with Pilate, urging him to condemn the innocent one in judgment unjustly. The Egyptian woman brazenly cried out to her husband, urging him in anger to punish that chaste man as though he were corrupt. The whole truth was hidden from the Egyptian man, for he did not know that Joseph was being wronged when he accused him. The assembly was wicked: even when the judge perceived what was happening at the trial, it felt no shame that would make it restrain its oppression of the upright one. No one had endured an unjust judgment like the Savior. Everyone who is wronged finds comfort in him, if he has discernment. Through the sufferings of the Son all the righteous were comforted, and through his wounds they found relief in their afflictions. Whenever falsehood contended with the upright, the oppression of the Son comforted them through its hidden meaning. Joseph was unjustly detained for judgment, but because he bore the image of the Son, he was at peace within himself. He was condemned while innocent, and envy pursued him while he was upright. He resembled his Lord, in whom all oppression reached its culmination. His master's anger also blazed against him, against the young man, because of these lying words that had been spoken. He who was not contemptible was made contemptible before those who heard them. But the one watching this trial was God. His master became angry and sent him to prison, so that through this too Christ's imprisonment and judgment might be proclaimed. Falsehood carried out its work against that upright man. It threw him into prison to be mistreated unjustly. Yet the image of our Lord did not cease winning victories, for even in prison his beauty shone upon the prisoners. The wronged man entered to be imprisoned without any guilt, as with the Son—for look, in the abode of the dead dwells the one who was born free. The Lord bestowed kindness and mercy on him in prison, for our Lord's entry into Sheol was portrayed in him. With that freedom full of beauty, Joseph entered, so that even in prison he might care well for those imprisoned there. In his soul the Only Begotten entered the abode of the departed, and visited them with care in their chambers. Through Joseph the prisoners found comfort from their troubles, and through our Lord the dead received hope of resurrection. Through Joseph, who was wronged, the one who had committed an offense took courage, knowing that he was imprisoned with a freeborn man and need not be distressed. Through that Son of the Living One, comfort was given to all the departed, because, though innocent, he entered prison among the guilty. The prison became a tomb for Joseph, and there he proclaimed how the Firstborn descends to Sheol among the departed. Look, Joseph is in Egypt's prison although he has done no wrong! It is as though someone were to say, “Our Lord is in Sheol, though he gives life to all.” In prison was the pure man, wronged though upright; and within the tomb was the Living One, killed though he is the giver of life. Look, in the abode of the dead is that freeborn one, as has been said. He resembles Joseph, who in his freedom cared for prisoners. You went mad, Egyptian woman, to imprison Joseph when he had done no wrong! Sin ran wild to kill our Lord, though he was innocent. Joseph did not neglect good deeds in prison, nor did our Lord cease bringing hope within the tomb. Imprisoned, he wisely cared for those who were imprisoned. He resembled his Lord, who died and raised those who were dead. That Egyptian woman desired Joseph, and because he was pure, she unjustly imprisoned him because he had escaped her desire. Sin, too, was jealous of our Lord, and because she had been put to shame, she crucified him on the wood because he was free from any involvement with her. Yet our Lord did not relinquish victory even in his death, nor did Joseph abandon freedom even in imprisonment. Come, see Joseph as he tended those who were imprisoned, and look at Christ as he preached to those who were dead. This radiance cast its dawning light upon the Hebrew, and through his wisdom the prison was illuminated by him. The likeness of our Lord shone in him in every form, and it changed its beautiful appearances in him with every season. One symbol brought him to another throughout his journey, so that his beautiful qualities might multiply as they were arranged one after another. They marveled at him—the prisoners—at how wisely he managed things. The chief jailer made him chief over those who were imprisoned. Administration prospered in Joseph’s hands, for whatever he undertook or did was blessed. The Lord did not abandon that faithful man even in imprisonment, but granted him mercy and bestowed favor upon him who had been wronged. These righteous people are good, choice gold, and in trials they were refined as though in fire. God both disciplined and protected them, for wisdom was learned through discipline. Whenever he handed one of the righteous over to great humiliation, he in turn caused to spring up for him, from the very humiliation he had inflicted, exalted ranks. While they were persecuted, he protected them wherever they were. Had he wished, he could also have kept them from being persecuted. He allowed them to be persecuted while he loved them, because persecution benefits the soul when it is steadfast. He cast Jonah from the ship into the sea as though he had no pity, and then protected him in the heart of the seas as a beloved one. He drove the young men into captivity in Babylon as though he had no mercy, but rescued them from the flame and showed his love. He relaxed his hand, and they imprisoned Daniel in the pit; yet, showing that he was not neglectful, he subdued the lions before him. He led Abraham away from his family to the land of Canaan, and after he had suffered hardship, he promised him, “Your descendants will inherit it.” He bound Isaac and brought him up, placing him upon the burnt offering; and just as the knife was about to reach his neck, he redeemed him with a ram. He yoked Jacob to the humiliation of hired service, but set apart and gave him the spotted sheep, sustaining him with his wages. He brought weariness and toil upon them, along with hardship, but he did not forsake them or leave them without help. He trained them through great hardship and trials, for the soul has something to gain from hardships. Yet he did not remove his help far from them, lest, when he withheld it from them, they should grow weak. How many trials came upon Joseph, that choice gold! Yet the Lord did not allow him to fail when he was tested. He became a slave, yet he gave orders to masters. He was enslaved, yet he managed his masters’ household. He entered prison, and authority was given to him. He was imprisoned, yet he managed affairs, for the Lord was with him wherever he went. Indeed, Joseph entered prison and exercised authority there. In one respect he was dishonored, and in another he was honored. He was imprisoned like a slave, yet he gave orders like a free man. He was counted among the prisoners, yet authority accompanied him. Through discipline he was becoming wise in spiritual matters, and through authority he was learning about help. This is the path of both the first and the last, and honor and disgrace are encountered on it by anyone who travels along it. Both blame and praise are found within it, for the one who governs is wise at heart and makes everyone wise. Where he disciplines, he seeks to strike down evil passions, so that through discipline he may put them to sleep in the faithful. And where he gives support, his providence desires to strengthen, so that through confidence he may awaken the soul without doubt. Whenever a passion is about to awaken in the soul, disgrace strikes it down. When it sinks and grows weak, praise springs up to comfort it. If he sees dregs in the soul, he arranges trials, so that, as it suffers through them, whatever does not belong to it may flee. And if he sees that it is again inclining toward doubt, through his help he gives it some support and encourages it. There are also times when the soul rejoices in good things, and he strikes it so that it may wake up and guard the wealth it possesses. There are also times when he seeks to rebuke the love of glory, and he stirs up disgrace against the honored to strike them down. For this is a path of praise and blame, and honor and disgrace are handed out along it, as it is written. Who has ever governed so well as God? In everything he does, he seeks to benefit the one who loves him. He granted Joseph authority among the Egyptians. He struck him severely, and then entrusted him with leadership. He trained him through hardship and trials of every kind, [?] a lax thought springing from freedom. He brought him to trial, and then made him a high judge, so that he would be patient in judgment, lest there be injustice. He made him suffer oppression while reserving leadership for him, so that when oppressed people approached him, he would work to rescue them. Falsehood attacked him, though he had not provoked it, so that he would be truthful when investigating what was right. He entered prison so that through this he might learn wisdom, so that, as a ruler, he would guard against injustice toward prisoners. He confined him in a pit while preparing a chariot for him, so that in his greatness he would remember whoever was lowly. He brought him under the yoke of slaves so that he would learn there that a master ought to have compassion on his workers. He was reserved for honor, yet he subjected him to disgrace on every pretext, so that when he was honored, he would give thanks for his deliverance and not become conceited. He cauterized all the soul’s passions through every kind of trial, so that nothing hateful would stir within it in that greatness. That free man was tested in the rank of slaves so that he would take care to free all who were imprisoned. He resembles his Lord, who suffered and was tested so that through this he might help those who are tested, as it is written. His story is a sea, and how can I rise out of its billows? For wave after wave tosses me onward to travel through it again. His wealth is immense, and I am too weak for its trade. I cannot carry his treasures, because they are so many. So I will take a single coin at a time for my need. Blessed is the rich one who gives every day to those who ask him. Here ends the fifth homily of Saint Mar Jacob.
The Sixth Homily on Joseph
The Sixth Homily on Joseph: When He Interpreted the Dreams of the Two Men Who Were Imprisoned

Anyone who dares to paint the sun is badly mistaken, for he has no colors suited to its splendor. Perfect beauty cannot, with inferior colors, is bounded. And how can the finger of an artist portray him? Joseph’s story is like the sun, and how, then, can I contain his story on the page of a discourse? I do not know. The sun’s heat is beyond the power of painters, and when they paint it, its heat cannot be confined within their pigments. The image of the Son that Joseph put on is beyond all bounds. How much can I say about what is great and cannot be bounded? Living fire is kept within his story, and just as I seek to approach him, it flares up within me with its heat. Joseph’s story cannot be told except through our Lord, for through him Joseph conquered the land of Egypt, to which he had gone down. He carried the King’s standard to be set up among the Egyptians, and the awe-inspiring sign conquered the land that had been rebellious. The Son of God placed his testimony in Joseph, his servant, and sent him to Egypt to paint an image there through wonders. Mysteries accompanied him with honor along the whole journey as he went down, and all the sufferings that befell him, he wandered through them. Even in prison, the mysteries of our Lord did not depart from him, for in the prison he depicted the likeness of the crucifixion. He stood between the two servants of the king who were with him, just as the Son had two robbers crucified with him. The king’s cupbearer and baker had been imprisoned with him, so that even in prison they might portray the Son through a mystery. Both of them dreamed dreams at the same time, and these distressed them, so that Joseph might interpret and explain what would happen to them. Joseph went in to visit them as usual and found them mourning because of their dreams. The diligent man began to ask them about their sadness: “What is the reason for your distress?” For he took care to visit those who were imprisoned, and like a caretaker he supplied their needs. With his gentle words he comforted them in their troubles, for he did not neglect to ask about their lives. He saw that Pharaoh’s servants were mourning, and in his concern he approached them to ask: “Why are you so downcast today? I see a new sorrow in your faces.” They said, “Dreams have worn us down, and we are terrified. We have been greatly troubled by visions in the night. A scourge was sent to us in sleep, together with turmoil. A dream has disturbed us, and there is no interpreter to comfort us. The vision is difficult, and there is no one here to explain it. That is why sorrow is tormenting us and we are downcast.” Joseph said, “Dreams belong to God, and he is the one who can reveal their meanings.” It was fitting for that wise man to proclaim in the land of Egypt that interpretations belong to the Lord. In a land rebellious against right guidance, he openly spoke God’s name so that God would help him. He first ascribed the interpretation to the Lord, saying that it belonged to him, so that when the dreams were interpreted, he would receive the praise for it. “Dreams belong to God; tell them to me.” They began to recount their visions to him. Here Joseph was wholly stamped with the image of the Son as he stood between the robbers on Golgotha. Joseph made a distinction between these servants of the king, decreeing life for one and death for the other. He brought one into the royal palace and before Pharaoh, and handed the other over to become food for the birds. Who could paint so beautiful an image as Joseph painted of Christ in all His beauties. / The Savior stood between robbers on Golgotha, / and condemned one and acquitted the other, just as Joseph also did. / He brought one into the kingdom through faith, / and cast the other into Gehenna because he took offense. / To this one he said, “You will be with me in the garden of Eden,” / while he left the other beside those who crucified him, amid great mockery. / One is called an heir, a companion, and a son of the kingdom; / the other joins the blasphemers, the sons of the left. / Joseph himself also proclaimed these things through wonders. He had made a chasm between the right and the left. / He granted the king’s banquet to the chief cupbearer, / just as the Son gave the kingdom to the one on the right. / To the chief baker he gave crucifixion through the interpretation of dreams. / This is what happened to that robber on the left. / Through Joseph’s mouth, death and life were appearing, / and through interpretation he had authority to give life and to kill. / In our Lord’s word, too, the kingdom was appearing, / for he has authority to give life to whoever asks him for it. / Sleep and night gave visions to Pharaoh’s servants, / and Joseph had authority over their dreams, to interpret them. / The robbers too saw Christ in the sleep of death, / and he interpreted for them which one would die and which one would live. / In bread and wine were death and life for the king’s servants— / a dream that is a mystery of the body of the Son of God. / The bread was one, and two interpretations were hidden in it: / it brought one into the king’s house and crucified the other. / Through bread and wine that interpreter gave life and killed, / for he was wise and drew an image of the Son of God. / Our Lord’s body was depicted in these dreams, / for he decreed death, and he gave life to whoever asked him for it. / The one crucified in disgrace took his place between the robbers, / and killed and gave life like Joseph, the interpreter of dreams. / As though out of sleep, the robbers recounted on their crosses / words resembling the dream that Pharaoh’s servants had seen. / One was saying from the right, “Remember me, my Lord.” / The other cried out from the left, “Come down from the wood!” / In one, faith blazed with love for the Son; / in the other, there blew a spirit of taking offense at the Savior. / One confessed that Jesus was king even when they crucified him, / and pleaded, “In your kingdom, remember me, my Lord.” / The other said, “If it is true that he is the Son of God, / let him save himself and save us too, so that we may believe in him.” / To one, a revelation of faith was being sent, and, as though in a dream, he saw that Christ was God. / But doubt entered the other like a vision, / so that he denied the Son, saying that because he was crucified, he was not king. / An interpreter was needed between them, / to explain to each one what would happen to him. / Then the Lord of Joseph spoke from the top of the wood, / to reveal the interpretation of the words that had been spoken. / To one he said, “You will be with me in the garden of Eden.” / But the other he rejected, to be judged with those who crucified him. / To one robber he explained that he would enter the royal house, / and to the other he explained that in justice he belonged on the left. / He fulfilled the mystery that Joseph had woven among the Egyptians: / he gave life to one and crucified the other through the interpretation of a dream. / To one he granted the king’s banquet along with his service, and to the other he explained the terrible death that would befall him. / Through the dream Joseph was given authority to give life and put to death, / and in his interpretations everything happened just as he said it would. / He interpreted and brought one into the king’s house, and his word stood. / Again he decreed, brought the other out, and hung him on a cross, and no one restrained him. / On the tips of his lips, death And life on both sides. Wherever his word required it, events unfolded according to his interpretation. To one he gave service to the king, and it was granted to him; and to the other, his execution came from the interpretation, and he met death. He also had authority to give life and decree death, for he bore his Lord’s likeness in prison, and it made him wise. The Ruler of all gave him a word of command, so that through his words he might interpret and explain life and death. He bore the great image of the Son of God in the house of prisoners, and through it he spoke with authority to those who were imprisoned. From it he received a word possessing authority, so that even over the dreams of the night it might extend its command. He became a judge and released prisoners through the interpretation of their dreams. One he put to death, and the other he restored to his service. Pharaoh was silent, while Joseph gave commands within his kingdom about what would happen to these servants of his who were imprisoned. Justice came by night to settle their sentences, and in another language it explained the sentence. But no one knew what it had said except Joseph, for he was a confidant, and it was the King’s image that he bore with honor. From the dream he heard speech foreign to the Egyptians, and he explained the judgment and how it would be settled by its decrees. Three days, he interpreted, Joseph said, they would remain imprisoned, so that the Son’s burial might be plainly revealed: three days in the place of darkness, as one might say. The mystery of the Son, who justly acquitted and condemned. The three days Joseph had interpreted were completed, and Pharaoh acted just as the dream had shown at that time. Joseph had settled the whole judgment before it came to pass: what the dream decreed, he had interpreted, and Pharaoh fulfilled it. Through our Lord, Joseph’s story grew beyond those who tell it; however much they may say, it cannot be told as it truly is. Light dawned within him from that Sun of Righteousness, and therefore he shone brightly even in prison. Confined in the prison, he settled the judgment of the royal household, and he had authority to interpret the hidden things of dreams. He was kept in prison, while rulership was kept for him. While he was being beaten down, he was being raised toward leadership. Although he earnestly pleaded with the king’s cupbearer, saying, “Remember me,” he did not remember him, because it was not the time for his leadership. For it would have been too small a thing for him to come out through interpreting servants’ dreams. He remained in prison so that also for the king himself he might become an interpreter. The revelation of his wisdom came through a great occasion, so that the land might recognize how much authority he had over hidden things. He became an interpreter for the servants of the king, and it amounted to nothing. He was being kept for the king’s revelation, through which he would come out. Those thirty years of the Son before his revelation were being completed in him in prison, and then he would come out. The mystery kept Joseph concealed in prison until that full measure of thirty was completed. For this reason the chief cupbearer had forgotten him, for Truth had directed him not to speak before the proper time. The seed lay hidden, and all trials battered it, until the season for fruit arrived, and then it sprouted. He covered the image until all its colors were gathered, and then he brought it out so that the land might see how beautiful it was. He remained in prison until all the mysteries were completed, and then he came out, taking possession of the land as its lord. For thirty years our Lord walked among those on earth, and afterward he arranged his revelation before John. Although he could have acted this way earlier, his own. He maintained an order for his incarnation, so that it would not be disrupted. Joseph was kept until he reached this measure, and then he would go out to oversee the land to which he had been sent. He entered prison and sat waiting until that interval in which leadership reaches maturity was completed. For this reason too, the mystery confined him in a hidden place, so that he would not appear among the Egyptians except at his appointed time. Frost was holding back the seed so that it would become firmly rooted, so that it would not put out a shoot in December, but in May. The young man was kept until the appointed time, and then he would appear. For this reason, throughout all those times he was held back. From his youth the beauty of the Son blossomed in him, but frosts covered him so that he would not appear before the fulfillment. Already he had been honored by the dreams he saw, and they were about to reveal him. But the mystery covered him and hid him in Egypt while he grew. He had entered a house of slavery to work, and he became renowned there. But because his time had not arrived, they imprisoned him until it arrived. He was in prison, and he distinguished himself by interpreting dreams. But so that he would not come out, the matter was forgotten until its appointed time. The beauties of the Son burned within him, seeking to appear, but he covered them through various circumstances, waiting for the right opportunity. So that he would reach thirty years of age, he was delayed; then his administration would be revealed before the eyes of many. Whenever he was about to blossom, something held him back because he was young, so that through these restraints he would reach the time of maturity. And when all the colors of the great image had been gathered together, a great occasion called him into the open, so that he would appear. Pharaoh slept and saw a dream full of wonder, so that the Hebrew might come, interpret it, and take possession of the land. Sleep overtook him, and visions of the night rushed upon him, so that he would need an interpreter and Joseph would come. The One wise in heart, through the various circumstances he arranged, was subduing the fierce peoples in their lands. Through a dream he subjected both the Babylonians and the Egyptians, so that the might of their dominions would bow before the Hebrews. Daniel too distinguished himself by interpreting dreams, and the kings of Babylon bowed before him in their splendor. Joseph had done this very same thing among the Egyptians: he interpreted dreams and became lord of the whole land. The Hebrews were captives and exiles in foreign lands, yet their wisdom overcame kings and rulers. The Lover of humanity arranged things this way in his wisdom, so that it would serve the welfare of the whole community. The Hebrews were captives, yet they made their captors dependent on them, so that when dreams troubled them, they would seek help from the Hebrews; and so that, when profound things were revealed, it would become clear that the Lord has authority over hidden things and can bring them to light. And when hidden mysteries are explained by the Hebrews, the earth will recognize that their God is greater than all. Through revelations he humbles the arrogance of kings, so that they must depend on an interpretation before they find relief. He gave the captives authority over hidden things, so that when kings were tormented by dreams, they could give them rest. He made kings dependent on Hebrew interpreters, so that their need would be met by their own slaves; so that when a king was obliged to seek help from a captive, he would know that he too needed assistance. And when it was seen that he also had authority over hidden things, the world would recognize that he was the one who commanded visible things as well. The kings who, while awake, had conquered lands Through dreams at night he would subjugate the members of his people. When they triumphed among the legions and won victory, they returned bound by visions and asked for help. He took Daniel captive from his own country to the land of Babylon, and dreams came and took the king captive from his own bed. Out came the captive and rescued the king from the visions. He was obliged to bow down to the man who had been driven into exile. He made both sides dependent, each on the other, so that they would know that one alone supplies all needs. Kings depend on the interpretation of their visions, and interpreters on the document granting their freedom. Joseph was enslaved and greatly in need of freedom, and Pharaoh was distressed over his dream, needing it interpreted for him. Both needed to receive support from one another: the one to be freed, and the other to learn what his dream meant. Joseph was being kept to interpret the dream and through it be revealed, so that at his revelation Egypt would be stirred when he gave the interpretation. Pharaoh indeed fell asleep, and a dream came and set out its visions, making him dependent on an interpretation he did not know. Pharaoh saw himself standing beside the river, and there were seven fine, fat cows. They were beautiful and fat and strong, grazing there in the meadow he saw beside the river. Then seven ugly cows came up after them, ugly in appearance, with little flesh on them, and weak. There the thin cows ate the fat ones. Pharaoh awoke, terrified by the vision. He was seized with amazement at the new vision shown to him. He wondered what that revelation might mean, and while his thoughts in the night carried him toward its interpretation, he sank into sleep, and another dream came in to meet him. Again he saw a stalk with seven plump ears of grain, and after them another seven were coming up, thin ones. These gloomy-looking ears swallowed the good ones. Pharaoh awoke, and it had been a dream; amazement seized him. A revelation had come in and drawn for him a picture of things to come, but he had no eye that could discern it clearly. The vision troubled him, and he rose bewildered from his bed. He needed an interpretation that he might obtain from the wise men. The king's spirit was agitated by the vision he had seen, and he gathered all the magicians to disclose his dream. He summoned the wise men of all Egypt for an interpretation. He told them, but there was no interpreter to explain it to him. The dream bound him in ignorance, and he was agitated. He called on sorcery to release him, but it could not. The magicians came to investigate what the king's dream meant, but they could not discover the reason for the matter or its interpretation. A search for the interpretation was made on the left. He told them, but there was no interpreter to explain it to him. A search was made on the left for the interpretation, but it was unable to interpret a dream that came from the right. Demons were sent to investigate the reason for the dream, but because God had sent the dream, they did not understand it. The mystery was hidden from Satan and his servants: the Lord had sent Pharaoh's dream to be shown to him. From God came the revelation of true things, and the Evil One did not know how to interpret the hidden things. All sorcery failed to provide an interpretation, for the king's dream was hidden from it, and it could not discover it. The dream, which came from God, was reserved for the Hebrew, so that he might impart his Lord's teaching When he interpreted, the wisdom of all Egypt had been put to shame, because Pharaoh’s dream had not been interpreted by its wise men. Truth did not summon him— Joseph—to come from the beginning. It delayed for him so that all the wise men would be tested. It concealed his story and did not allow him to be revealed, so that sorcery would enter the royal palace and be put to shame. If Joseph had entered to interpret from the beginning, neither the sorcerers nor the wise men would have been exposed. For they would have said, “If Joseph had not interpreted it, we ourselves knew how to interpret the dream as he did.” For this reason, until all of them had gone in and come out, no mention was made of Joseph coming to interpret. Through his dream the king had scorned them as liars, and then he became aware that the truthful man should come to him. When they had all been questioned and had proved unable to understand, the king’s cupbearer remembered Joseph and his interpretations. The time had arrived for him to leave prison and be raised marvelously to a position of authority. He had also completed the full measure of thirty years, and the figure of the Son was moving to reveal itself. The cupbearer then approached and told Pharaoh about Joseph. The king sent and released the wronged man so that he could come to him. A woman had imprisoned him, and a king released him as he came out, so that he would be exalted in place of his humiliation among the Egyptians. Let anyone who is wronged look to Joseph and take comfort, and, if he is discerning, endure injustice without grumbling. Have people wronged you? Look to God, who is not unjust. Do not devise ways to make it known that you have been wronged. If you wish to please God, discerning person, count the injustice people do you as a share of the virtues within you. Do not wear yourself out venting your feelings about being wronged, lest the virtue that has become entwined within you be rubbed away. If you affirm that God exercises providence, why trouble yourself to vent your feelings when you are wronged? Let Joseph be like a mirror for all who are wronged, and let them find comfort in him against the insults of their oppressors. Injustice imprisoned him, but his judgment was issued in righteousness, so that he would come and become lord over Egypt, which had wronged him. Like a physician, he entered the king’s presence to examine his pain and apply a bandage suited to his wound. But how he entered, and what it was that he said when questioned, requires time to recount at length. Keep the memory of his beautiful story in your minds, and I will keep the appointment of the discourse at the point where it has paused. Look, he has entered Pharaoh’s presence to be questioned about hidden things. Blessed is the one who revealed to him the king’s mysteries and their interpretations.
The Seventh Homily on Joseph
The Seventh Homily on Joseph, by Saint Mar Jacob: When He Left Prison, Entered Pharaoh’s Presence, and Interpreted the Dreams He Had Seen

The mysteries of our Lord have marked out a path for me among the scriptural readings, so that through them I may journey to the appointed subject of the discourse about the Only-Begotten. It is about him, the Son, that the books of prophecy are written. There is no page among the scriptural readings that does not bear his image. He is the cause of every revelation of truth, and everything that is apart from him is falsehood. He enabled the prophets to understand hidden things, and he revealed the depths to the seers. He ordained interpretations for dreams from the Father’s house, and he enriched the discerning with understanding. He is the truth, and everything true has been spoken through him. And if Any word that did not come forth through him is false. He made his servant Joseph wise among the Egyptians, and from him Joseph received enlightenment concerning revelations. For he was depicted in him, and his testimony was also placed in him. Therefore Joseph subdued the whole country through his wisdom. For if Joseph had not borne the image of his Lord, he would not have gained authority over hidden and visible things. Dreams confronted him, and he interpreted them clearly; turbulent crises, and he passed through them peacefully; authority, and he exercised it wisely. For in every circumstance the image of the Son grew greater in him. He subdued the land in both hidden and visible things, for the King's purpose was revealed in his wisdom. First dreams submitted to him, and then people; and visions honored him, and afterward he was honored by the Egyptians. He became a ruler over revelations, to administer them, and afterward he was established over the affairs of government. He conquered the realm of dreams through the knowledge given to him, and then Egypt feared him, and he became its lord. Until they saw that he had authority over visions of the night, they did not make him ruler over them to govern them. Until he pursued dreams and interpreted them, the Egyptians did not give him their hand so that he could subject them. For they said, “If he has authority over a dream of the night, what people will not obey his awesome power? Who is so much swifter than a dream that he could escape him? Even if he flies like a vision, he would catch him.” He was led from hidden things to visible things, because he had been sent by God to administer the country. First he entered and learned the mysteries of God's household, and afterward he received authority to become lord over Pharaoh's household. Pharaoh summoned him like a physician to examine his pain, and, as he had sought, he received healing and then submitted. The king had seen a vision in the night, and it had greatly troubled him. Joseph had entered to interpret the hidden things. The preceding discourse had progressed this far, and silence seized me, but now I have been stirred to speak. Now, word, you should hasten to the reading, and let the hearing of the ear incline [?] toward understanding. If you do not gain discernment for yourself as you listen, what benefit can you find in paying attention? Let both speech and hearing hasten toward benefit. And this is the word by which all discernment is stirred. My concern is not to tell how Pharaoh saw a dream; I am compelled to bring to light the wondrous mystery enacted through it. It was not Joseph's interpretation of the dream that was a marvel. Wonder seized me because his interpretation itself needs to be interpreted. So I will speak about the dream as an actual event, and then return to speak of it spiritually. Joseph entered, and Pharaoh began to speak: “I have dreamed a dream, and there is no interpreter to explain it to me.” The king acknowledged that there was no interpreter among the Egyptians, so that the wisdom of the Hebrew might be exalted. He disparaged all the wisdom of the Egyptians when he said, “I have dreamed a dream, and there is no interpreter.” Joseph began to offer help, and then he interpreted. For he said, “I will not give Pharaoh an answer of peace without the Lord.” He drove flattery out of the royal household, so that he might speak with integrity of soul, without fear. “I will not,” he said, “give Pharaoh an answer of peace without the Lord.” By this he showed that he would not submit to showing favoritism. Before interpreting the king's dream, he began to rebuke him. “For if God has decreed harm for you, I will not conceal it.” In this too he showed his truthfulness before giving the interpretation, so that he would not be compelled to conceal the truth and show favoritism. His words were clear and did not incline toward falsehood. To show that he would not interpret except through the Lord, he first bound that interpretation to God, so that Pharaoh would lift his eyes toward him when he spoke. The king said, “I saw myself standing on the riverbank, and there were seven cows, fat ones, grazing. Then after them I saw seven ugly ones, and the bad ones ate the good ones as I watched. I went back to sleep and saw seven good ears of grain. Then after them seven thin ones came up, and these shriveled ones swallowed the full ones that were there. All that goodness remained within that badness.” Joseph heard Pharaoh’s dream and understood it, and readily began to interpret it in terms of what would happen: “God has shown Pharaoh what he is preparing to do. Both dreams have one meaning and one interpretation. The seven cows are years of abundance, and the seven ears of grain are likewise good years. The seven bad cows are also years, and these thin ears of grain mean exactly the same thing. The Lord is bringing great abundance throughout the land, and afterward there will be famine and scarcity. In these first seven years that I mentioned, the land throughout Egypt will pour forth crops without limit. Afterward there will be a famine unlike any other, and the great abundance will be forgotten in the famine that follows. The command came from God to show you. The dream was repeated twice so that you would believe. This is something firmly determined by God: there will be abundance, followed by famine throughout the land. Through the dream the Lord has sent you word of what he is doing, so that you may be prepared and manage the country wisely. Let Pharaoh seek a man who is wise and full of understanding to gather grain in the land during the years of abundance. Let provisions be stored in the land for the coming famine, for the dream has alerted you to prepare for this too.” Joseph had begun to give orders among the Egyptians, for his time had come to take up his authority. They had summoned him from prison merely to interpret dreams, but he began arranging what should happen in the kingdom. The wise-hearted man interpreted the vision, but that was not enough for him: he was also arranging what should be done about the coming famine. “Let the king take,” he said, “one fifth from the land, so that grain may be kept in the country for the coming famine.” Before they had given him authority, he assumed authority over the king’s household, and he was giving orders about how things should be done throughout the land. Egypt marveled at how wise this Hebrew was: he interpreted dreams and advised how to put the country in order. Pharaoh was astonished at him, his interpretations, and his advice, and marveled at how discerning he was in his wisdom. He began to say, “Who is like this man in all the land, understanding and full of the spirit that comes from God?” Authority dawned upon the wronged man in the king’s household, and he began to honor and exalt the man who had been humbled. Pharaoh said, “You shall have authority over my royal household, and you shall be lord and judge over all Egypt. By my throne alone will I be greater than you, and in nothing else. My whole dominion shall be subject to you as to a lord.” Truth had dawned and given Joseph leadership. And he made him a lord, the one who had been persecuted throughout his journey. The waves that had battered him from every side grew calm, and he began to gather wealth greater than the storms. The envy born of deceit and the accuser left him, along with daily oppression and persecution at every moment. The tree stirred into life to yield the fruit that had been hidden within it, and frost, cold, and all the winds ceased to trouble it. The king put a ring on his hand and made him a lord, as one might say, “Let the seal of my kingdom be yours.” He put on a garment of fine linen and was raised to leadership, and the whole country knelt and bowed before him as before a king. They placed a gold necklace around his neck to give him splendor, and proclaimed before him, “Father and lord of all Egypt!” On the king’s chariot he sat to make a tour of Egypt, and the word of his authority spread throughout the country. It was fitting for him to become a master over masters, for he had practiced no deceit among his masters when he was enslaved. Leadership suited that wise man, who had conducted himself carefully everywhere. It was right for him to rule over a kingdom, for he had first built himself a wall of vigilance. It is a great thing for someone to govern himself well, like someone who has built a great city with seven walls. For someone to subdue confused impulses is greater than for someone to conquer many lands and the peoples within them. Whoever has overcome his passions is like someone who has triumphed over captors; he has rescued his soul from overthrow, as one rescues a city. A city does not depend on guards as much as the soul depends on vigilant thoughts. See, the wise man brings peace to his city, as has been said. But greater than he is the one who settles his soul in peace. For someone who has managed to govern himself without blame, even a royal city would be a small thing to govern. Authority, then, was fitting for Joseph, who had managed himself well from his youth. Someone who has not learned to govern himself— how could he possibly manage others? It is fitting that this man should rule over many: the one who has mastered his own will through good deeds. Joseph was able to govern both himself and others well and to manage wisely. Because he had been a righteous teacher to himself, kings accepted his teaching and submitted to him. Leadership therefore suited this man, so that all Egypt should run after him and submit to him. This man was truly raised up onto the chariot. Through strength of soul, he had first ridden uprightly. He was exalted, and leadership suited him. And when he was brought low, he did not complain against God. Through these experiences that befell him, he was distinguished as someone capable of being governor of all Egypt. By being a righteous slave, he gave proof that he could be raised above slaves without becoming conceited. In that humiliation, his discernment had been revealed: even if he were exalted, he would not harm his companions. If he conducted himself uprightly while he was a slave, how much more justly would he conduct himself as a master! Choice gold had entered the furnace of every trial, and because it was choice, kings honored it upon their crowns. It was fitting for someone who governed himself well to hold authority over many in his hand. It befits the one who [?], being above reproach. His word runs freely and is not despised by those who hear it. A reprover is feared when he himself is free from blame. Let each person do only those things that he himself demands, everyone. Whoever has labored and adorned himself with good deeds ought also to be an example to others. Whoever has exerted himself and kept himself away from disputes ought also to judge others uprightly. If someone has not practiced authority over himself, he stumbles when he is entrusted with command. If his own bodily members do not obey him so that he can bring them into submission, with what faculties can he subdue the brutish? His own have rebelled against him, and those who are not his own—how will they obey? Let him gain control of his own, and then seek to control those of others as well. Someone who rebels against correction—how can his word be effective when he corrects the unjust? Authority, then, was fitting for Joseph, and it was easy for him to correct others because he was righteous. He cleared himself of blame, and then advanced to being appointed over the land as one who demanded good deeds. Solomon pronounced woe upon the city whose king is a child, and whose officials eat in the morning like little children. This is the soul that inclines toward desires and occupies itself with them, and is stirred up by impetuous thoughts about evil things. Blessed is the city whose king is wise and freeborn! This is the soul whose trust is placed in upright conduct. Whoever has governed this city without blame finds nothing too difficult to govern. Here Joseph trained himself in uprightness, and truth took hold of him so that through him it might provide for all Egypt. He richly supplied himself with love for the Lord, and went out to supply the land of Egypt with crops. Administration became easy for that wise man, because his soul's view of affairs was upright. He became the steward of the household, governing his fellow servants, and it was fitting for him because his compassion was abundant. In the time of plenty he was making provision for the coming famine, for the great responsibility for the whole land rested on him. A dream revealed to him the distress that would come upon the land, and in his wisdom he fought against the famine. The vision came and brought news of the coming calamity, and Joseph began to forge the weapons he would need. The wise man marshaled great supplies against the famine, so that the land would not shrink from it when it fought. As though laying an ambush, he stored abundant grain in the storehouse, to establish a battle line against the time of scarcity. The produce of the earth he heaped up abundantly in buildings, so that it would be available for the hungry and they would not be handed over to distress. He went out through the land to gather the grain of the earth. Heights and valleys poured forth crops on every side. The earth's produce streamed toward that wise man, for it was good for the earth that he administered it wisely. While he was amid [?], his eye was fixed on famine, for he firmly trusted that revelation from God. He stored up and heaped together all the abundant crops, so that the grain he gathered would provide for the hungry. The fields of Egypt poured forth abundance before Joseph, so that the land might hold its head high under his rule. The earth's womb brought forth all its rich produce before him, so that he might lay up in the land a great treasure filled with abundance. He gathered grain beyond counting, more than the sand, and filled the land with abundance to overcome the coming famine. He stocked the land with provisions. many, so that it would not be devastated when the time of famine came upon it. The seven good years came to him, just as he had interpreted them, and with his careful attention he managed them wisely. He was discerning, giving each season its due, so that whenever the various seasons came upon him, he could provide for them. In the time of plenty he did not forget the famine that was approaching, and to meet it he greatly increased the stores throughout Egypt. Let anyone entrusted with leadership look at Joseph, at how vigilant he was in managing good things. That wise man was a mirror filled with beautiful things, and anyone who looks at him discerningly is adorned by him. Anyone who is not the head of a people is the head of his own soul, and he is required to take care of himself. Whoever subdues these brutish impulses of his has a great victory, like the head of a people whose conduct is upright. If you have not been entrusted with many people to settle their affairs, here are your thoughts: if you are wise, manage them. You are your own head, and your conduct lies within your own will. The territory you govern—your own self—is not small. In it you have great toil and hard labor. Even if you work at it night and day, you will barely master it. Your soul requires you to stay watchful over it and guard it. When you have kept it from evil things, your labor is great. If you are wise, govern one soul well, and never desire leadership, which is entirely anxiety. Every person is his own head and ruler, and when he governs himself well, he is victorious. Joseph himself also triumphed here in leadership, when he was able to keep himself from harm. He practiced leadership and authority over his own soul, and, as he wished, he guided it peacefully by his wisdom. His being raised up onto a chariot was nothing; his victory inside the bedroom was something great. The grain he gathered when he came to power has run out and is gone. But though the world should come to an end, his good name will not come to an end. The ring Pharaoh put on his hand is no longer here, but his vigilance has a great triumph throughout all generations. It was not the necklace around his neck that made him renowned on earth; his own chastity won triumph throughout the lands. These, then, are the precious things through which he became great. They are glorious for anyone who takes care to acquire them. Multiply, then, all our gains from his story. Throughout his whole story, he is entirely a store of good things. The story of the righteous greatly benefits all who hear it. Blessed is the Righteous One who crowned them in their contests.
The eighth discourse on Joseph.
The eighth discourse on Joseph and on the famine that occurred.

Joseph has opened for me a great door of discoveries. Through you, my Lord, I will enter and see the beautiful things arranged within him. Reveal something new that is not his own, and show it to me. Fill me with wonder, so that I may speak again about his victories. Yours, my Lord, are all the treasures that were hidden within him, and from them he brought out wealth for Egypt, to which he was sent. The poor man wore borrowed garments and became great through them, until the whole earth thought that he himself was rich. The mysteries of the Son supported him so that he could rise to greatness, and for that reason he attained all this authority. In his image there was a radiance borrowed from the Only Begotten, and for that reason his beautiful name shone over all creation. I will speak, then, about that Beauty who gave him beautiful things, while keeping the discourse in order throughout his way. He interpreted the king’s dream and rose to greatness through its interpretation. Yet from within the dream’s mystery another mystery was springing up. Joseph interpreted it in terms of events as they occurred in his time, but that interpretation needs a second interpretation. It is not because I am more skilled than Joseph that I have set myself to explaining the dream’s significance and its precise meaning. The cross revealed all mysteries and hidden things, and through it the concealed depths were explained. Since the coming of our Lord and down to the present, revelations have shone forth. There is nothing hidden with the Father that he has not given us. The beauty of colors can only be distinguished in the light, and the mysteries of the Son were only explained through his death. Who knew before his coming, so as to explain it, that our Lord’s body is nourishment for the world in its entirety? In whose mind had this dawned: that these beautiful qualities found in Joseph belonged to Christ? A further meaning remained stored in Pharaoh’s dream which had been interpreted, for there was no way for it to be explained before the coming. He saw seven fat cows beside the river, as if to speak of great abundance throughout the world. The human world itself, when interpreted, is a river, and generations pass like streams, one after another. It is a mighty current whose source begins with Adam. Like flowing water, it is renewed every day. Stand beside the river and look at those waters of yesterday: they have changed their place and are no longer there for you to see. Other waters appear to you today as you look, and these too hasten to pass on with their companions. The world itself also hurries to move toward its end. Like waters that rush downhill every day, the generations push one another onward, just as waves in a river hasten along their course. Look carefully, and you can discover that the world is a river that flows and passes away, moving onward with a mighty rush. The years are yoked like cows under a great yoke, drawing the world along so that it passes swiftly. Abundance and famine are arranged to come one after another, so that the world may learn about its Maker through his provisions. God painted a picture of the world for Pharaoh in a dream and called Joseph to explain its truths to him. Instruction shone clearly there, wisely proclaiming the world’s changing condition. The dream had stationed Pharaoh at a crossing, so that he might see the ages all passing away. It depicted abundance and famine before him so that he might become wise and remember the Provider all his days. He saw cows grazing in a meadow, as if to say that the world is a meadow and people wither like flowers. Today is the abundance that the Son of God has brought into the world. Let whoever is wise store up good things for himself. The body of the Son is a great harvest for whoever receives it, for a reserve of life for the new world is stored in it. Look, like Joseph, if you are wise, in the time of abundance, and go out and gather provisions for yourself, so that you may live on them. The grain Joseph gathered ran out, decayed, and vanished, but the body that lives forever is nourishment for whoever receives it. Keep this great provision within you for the last day, so that it may be available to you and you may live on it without end. Famine comes after this abundance that has come, just as Pharaoh saw clearly in the dream. In Gehenna a drop of water is a great thing, and whoever here Whoever does not prepare this for himself is destitute. In that affliction, a single crumb of life is abundance. Whoever is kept safe by it is nourished by it and is not tormented. To meet bodily hunger, Joseph took care to gather grain that lasts for a time, for life that lasts for a time, among the Egyptians. Jesus our King gave as nourishment his living body, to give life to souls and bodies in his new world. This is provision that not even Gehenna can destroy, for by its power it fights against the fire and extinguishes it. This is the drink that quenches the thirst of the soul that drinks it, so that it is not handed over to dwell among those who thirst in the flame. Receive the body and blood, O man, in faith, and tread upon the blazing fire and pass through it into the kingdom. Hide this leaven in your dough, O mortal, for in it there is life without end for whoever is worthy of it. This is a time of great abundance throughout the earth. Gather and increase for yourself enduring life while there is still opportunity. Look, discerning one, at that wonderfully wise man, Joseph, who fought against famine in the time of abundance. Whoever is wise like Joseph looks far ahead. He stored up provisions for himself while he still had control over his conduct. In the other world there is no harvest from free choice. This is the time when we can easily acquire every good thing. At that end, no one sows, because there is no opportunity. The end is harvest: everyone will gather all their crops. This is the time when whoever is diligent does business, gathering for himself provisions of life for the great world to come. The Son of God has increased the harvest among mortals. O diligent ones, fill your souls with new life. From his Father's house he freely grants everything that is asked for. He does not take payment from those who receive, as Joseph did. Joseph gave nothing of his own when he was distributing provisions, but our Savior gave his own body to the needy. Take care, then, O mortals, to gather enduring life, which, look, is now being given freely. Joseph, wise in heart, portrayed a good example for us, so that in the time of abundance we might thoughtfully remember famine. I will move through his story, which is full of beautiful things, briefly, for the discourse has called me to move toward its conclusion. Abundance had passed, and famine began to come upon the land. And he arose to provide for the whole world, this son of the Hebrews. Famine drew the countries to come to him, for his administration had distinguished him over many. The needy stood at his door to ask for food, because he could readily help them in their distress. The hungry of the earth ran after him so that he might satisfy them, for he had enough bread to sustain them. The poor turned from every direction toward the rich man, for he had great stores with which to provide for them. Lords and rulers lacked bread, while Joseph alone enjoyed great abundance. Blessed is he who made him triumph!
The Ninth Discourse on Joseph
The Ninth Discourse on Joseph and His Brothers, When They Went Down to Buy Grain, by the Holy Mar Jacob the Teacher

That handsome Joseph, who triumphed among the Egyptians, gave me abundant material in his story to speak about. He opened his Scripture reading and promised me discoveries. And now he sets me to work revealing the mysteries that were hidden in him. His story is a treasure, and he has opened it lavishly before me. Now he urges me to carry away as much from it as I diligently can. How much can I manage, and how long can I hold out, weak as I am? For the account of this man cannot be encompassed even in lengthy discourses. About him Had I undertaken to speak about him alone, perhaps I could have managed, or brought it to completion and an end. But since the mystery of the Son of God is attached to his story, I cry out openly that I cannot manage, because it is beyond me. Had he not resembled our Lord in his deeds, [?] I would have finished his discourse and his story in a few words. Had the likeness of the Son of God not been depicted in him, his story would have ended with a few details, and silence would have covered him. But because Christ is woven into him, he cannot be fully described in a discourse, for he is a great sea whose limits no one has ever reached. I will now proceed briefly with Joseph’s story, reserving the end of the discourse for the great mystery. The capable man arose to administer the land of Egypt, and the earth trembled in its need for him, seeking to come to him.
