They set out and gathered together, countries and cities, to receive from Joseph food to satisfy the hunger within them. He became a provider for the world, which was in need, and in the time of famine he kept it alive with food. The grain of all the wealthy men throughout the lands ran out, and Joseph’s [?] became renowned in every region. Then famine entered Judah, which denied the truth, to bring the treacherous brothers to the faithful man. Need came upon them and bound them bitterly, so that they would fall before him in homage against their will. For the day had come for the dreams and revelations to be clearly interpreted, just as they had been given. Old Jacob called his sons and sent them to the land of Egypt because of the famine that oppressed them. Need drew them and brought them to Joseph’s door, so that they might come and see that greatness which put them to shame. The envious men saw the envied young man who had been sold, holding the world in his power and governing it as its lord. They gazed at that freeborn man who had become a slave, who had been made lord over all Egypt and exercised authority in it. They saw him clothed in glory, renown, and authority, holding in his hand all the land’s bounty and wealth. He alone supplied the countries with food in abundance. He had a great harvest available, and no one else did. The doors of all the wealthy men were deserted, while his resounded with activity, and lords begged him to feed them. The dignitaries of the earth bowed before him so that he would keep them alive. Egypt and Philistia ran to his feet with their companions. Judah and Canaan and their inhabitants marveled at him. The greatness given to him suited him well, and leadership befitted him, as did authority. The lords of the land had become servants and obeyed him. He held power over the kingdom of Egypt and governed it. He was clothed in government and authority. The brothers saw their wronged brother in great glory, and they fell trembling on their faces before him. Bowing down were the withered, empty sheaves before Joseph’s sheaf, full of abundance, so that it would feed them. The stars saw him like a great day that had dawned, and they bowed before him as he covered them with his rays. There the interpretation of the dreams shone out clearly: the stars and the sheaves bowed to the young man in the gathering of his brothers. Heaven and earth honored him through their actions, and on every side they supported him so that he might rise to greatness. The Lord of creation gave him strength and mighty deeds, and through the produce of the heights and the depths he glorified and exalted him. The wrongdoers lay on their faces before Joseph, while the one who had been wronged He was high and exalted upon the chariot. That greatness, full of strength, was humbled and cast down before the humble man whom envy had pursued until he became great. They bowed down therefore, Joseph’s brothers, on their faces, and asked him for grain for the hungry people in their households. He saw them and recognized them clearly. He began to question them craftily: “Who are you? You are spies who have come to see the good things of the land. Your company is also known to be deceitful.” They said, “We are neither spies nor liars, but righteous men, sons of righteous men, and lovers of truth. Twelve of us were fathered by our aged father Jacob. Look, one is with him, one is lost to him, and ten are here.” Joseph dealt with them sternly and wisely, for the memory of the dreams stirred him to put pressure on them, so that the interpretation of the dream would be confirmed by his brothers’ bowing down, as they bent low and pleaded with him to release them. They bowed down to him and asked him to have mercy on them, just as the sheaves had bowed down to his sheaf in the dream while he slept. The lions were brought low and cast down, full of strength, before that lamb whom they had torn and cast away from their company. Joseph dealt harshly with them like a wise man, so that, as they bowed down to him, the dreams he had dreamed would find their fulfillment. That tribute which the dreams had granted him from his brothers—he demanded it of them, to receive it from them against their will. The dream had drawn up a written claim for homage and given it to him to demand from them. He showed a stern face until he received it. He was full of mercy and did not wish to harm them, but wanted the interpretation of his dreams to be confirmed. He showed them a face of anger and menace, so that, once what had been decreed had taken place, he could have mercy on them. “You are deceitful spies who have come to inspect the country.” They said, “We are not spies, but righteous men.” In his heart, Joseph gently mocked them: “How are they righteous, when they made a freeborn man a slave?” Look, their righteousness has been selling freeborn people from of old, and their wickedness crucified the Lord of freedom upon the wood. When they were righteous, they plotted against their brother, sold him, and drove him away; and when they were wicked, they insulted the Lord, flogged him, and crucified him. “We are righteous,” they were saying to the one who had been sold. From what had happened to him, he knew that they were not righteous. Under the yoke of slaves they yoked their brother—how, then, were they righteous? And toward their righteous father, [?] deceit, wickedness, and falsehood. Let us now speak words beyond the ordinary, which no one will heed unless his hearing is keen. It is clear that the Lord sent Joseph to the land of Egypt, and that the whole journey was his doing is also known. David said, “He sent a man ahead of them.” If he sent him, why are the man’s brothers guilty? Joseph also said, “For your sake the Lord sent me,” for he knew that his whole journey was God’s doing. And if Joseph acknowledged with his own mouth that the Lord had sent him, and David said, “He sent a man ahead of them,” who can find fault with a journey that came from God? For look, the Lord himself sent him there when he was sold. Shall we, then, praise Joseph’s brothers, who were envious and plotted deceitfully, lied to their father, sold their brother, and did all these things? Through their deceit, look, God’s purpose was carried out. Even through their wickedness the Lord’s work was accomplished. Through their envy they prepared the Lord’s way according to his will, so that Joseph went to the land of Egypt, as that he wanted. All the envy, deceit, and injustice of Joseph’s brothers had accomplished this: what God had decreed for the boy. And if this was the course of the Lord that they carried out when they sold him, let us praise them for becoming the cause of every benefit. Let us now stop praising good deeds, and let us become practitioners of deeds of injustice, boldly. But if praise is owed to Joseph’s brothers, then neither would Judas be condemned for selling his Lord. The death of the Son is a source of good for humanity. Let us therefore praise the crucifiers too for their deeds: Judas the deceitful, Caiaphas the unclean priest, and Annas the shameless, who crucified the Son—let us praise them! For they became a cause of hope for the whole world. For if the Son of God had not died, the world would not have risen. Then let us apply these same things to every evil, and when evil deeds are committed, let those who do them not be condemned. Relatives, friends, and confidants are what my discourse seeks: people who stand behind it and receive it with great love. Let those who commit injustice not be praised for their deeds, not even if every good thing flowed from them. The Lord is wise and has the power to bring every good thing out of evil and give it to humanity. Let him be praised, because whenever someone does evil to his neighbor, the Lord, who has the power, turns that very evil into good. Joseph’s brothers, for their part, made him a slave, but the Lord took him and made him lord over lords. The Judge, too, looks at the intention in which Joseph’s brothers persisted, and is angry when he questions them. He calls them to account according to their intention when they come before him. They have no share in the good things that came about through their hands. It is the evil intention that is judged by the just and upright one. For the intention itself is regarded as it really is. As envious men and sellers of free people, the Lord judges the brothers of Joseph for what they did to him. For the good that came about along his way when he was sold belonged to God, who can turn water into wine. But had they not sold him, that same good would still have been accomplished. And the Lord who sent him would have sent him according to his knowledge. And if the Lord found him as a slave and made him a king, could he not have exalted him while he was free? He brought him out of prison and gave him authority. Could he not, from his father’s house, have called him and honored him? He remembered him in the pit and set him on a chariot. If he had not fallen there, would he have forgotten him [?]? The disgrace of selling him is something the Lord calls them to account for, as though his whole course had taken place without him. They were unaware that the Lord had sent him when he was sold, and as though the Lord had not sent him at all, he judges them. Providence carried out its own work without them, and they are not praised for a good of which they were unaware. This is their own judgment from justice: they envied, schemed, lied, hated, sold, and drove away. They distressed their father, enslaved their brother, and wronged the truth. They angered the Lord and made a free man a slave. And as though the one who was sold had remained a slave forever, and as though he were bound, imprisoned, oppressed, and full of suffering, so they receive punishment from the Judge for what they did to him. But the fact that he was sent by God has nothing to do with them. Again, if you look discerningly from another perspective, you will see that his whole course belonged to God. And as though his brothers were not even aware When he was sold, the Lord arranged all the circumstances that occurred there. How fitting it was that he should become a slave, and how his path led to honor! He had been sold, and the whole providential arrangement concerning him was beautiful, as though it would not have taken place if he had not been sold. And so beautifully and orderly did the course of his journey unfold, as though anything missing from it would have been a defect. It is not that their wrongdoing was good, but that the Lord set his path in order. And see, it is beautiful and full of mysteries, like what happened to our Savior at the hands of those who crucified him: they seized him, imprisoned him, flogged him, crucified him, killed him, and buried him. All these things they did, though evil, were turned around and became hope and life for the world, so that it might live through them. Yet they receive punishment from justice because they crucified him, as though there had been neither life nor salvation in it. The crucifixion was their doing, but the salvation was his. And for this reason they have no share in the good that came about. Likewise, Joseph’s brothers are punished for having sold him. But his becoming great, and his being sent, are not their doing. Too lofty for my mouth is the account of this whole providential arrangement. I will leave it in silence, afraid, since it cannot be explained. The ear is accustomed to all these familiar sounds, and when it is not accustomed to something, even if someone says more, it does not enjoy it. Joseph’s brothers, then, lay facedown and pleaded with him, “We are honest men, my lord, and not spies.” They told him that they had a brother and a father, and he took the opportunity to see his brother Benjamin, whom he loved. “If you truly are honest men and sons of an honest man, give proof that you have not lied in what you have said. By this I will know whether all your words are true: when you bring me that brother of yours, the child of your father’s old age. Remain in prison, and send for the one you have spoken of and bring him. When he comes, it will be evident that you have not lied.” Joseph sent them away and wisely had them imprisoned, so that they would provide proof whether the words they had spoken were true. There he acted as their superior, though he did not hate them, so that by every means his brother might come, for he longed for him. Joseph’s brothers were frightened and bewildered by what had happened, for they were terrified by that command that the boy should come. They spent three days in prison, required to bring the boy Benjamin, as they had promised. Come, see now the wheel of time as it turns and makes what is lowly exalted: the boy who was envied, driven away, and sold has been made a lord, while those who sold him are imprisoned, suffering in a place of distress. The Lord turns all evil back upon those who do it, so that whoever digs a pit for his neighbor himself falls into it. He greatly honored the one who had been wronged and thrown into the pit, and bowed his oppressors down before him, to humble them. All these good things that were in Joseph were perceived by people in our Lord and his revelations, and all beautiful things converge on him from every side. Until the Son of God came and revealed himself, these beautiful things in Joseph seemed to be his own. But when he came, the world distinguished them and recognized that there were borrowed colors in his image, taken from Christ's. Let no one be astonished that I explain the symbols of our Lord that were clearly present in Joseph's life. Anyone who knows something that has happened should not be praised. But if he tells of it before it happens, he deserves praise. If there had been someone in creation who had seen beforehand Joseph's course and revealed its mystery, he would have been wise. If, before our Lord came to earth, someone had spoken these words about Joseph, he would have been knowledgeable indeed. But now that both the earlier and the later things have happened, who praises someone who understands their meaning? The human eye is entirely full of darkness at night but when daylight meets it, it clothes itself in light from it. And by that light which the eye receives from the day, the eye distinguishes beautiful things and forms as well. There is no way for the eye to distinguish colors at night until it clothes itself in strength and light from the day. Therefore the eye should never be praised for the light, but rather the light that gives it discernment. Our Lord, the daylight, dawned upon the world and enlightened everyone to distinguish the symbols that were there, as though they were colors. Who could have said, when Joseph was going down into the pit, that this young man was depicting the mystery of his Lord's death? Until the Son of God descended into the tomb and rose, no one examined the mystery and saw it so as to speak about it. Until Judas sold our Lord and received his price, it was not known why Joseph had been sold. Now that all creation has been enlightened concerning all the symbols, it is no cause for praise that we should tell them as they were enacted. When you hear the story of Joseph, who was envied and wronged, the story flashes forth toward that of Christ as it is told. As for daylight, even when the eye does not wish to see it, its very nature has a radiance that reveals itself to the eye. Even if the soul keeps silent about the mystery of the Son, it stirs the soul through itself to speak abundantly about him. Let us therefore tell of the things that happened, since they are clear—not because we have grasped hidden things through our wisdom. They are revealed already, so we should not seek to reveal them, but rather marvel at how clear and true they are. It was not our Lord who resembled Joseph the Hebrew, but Joseph who resembled our Lord in his deeds. After the Ancient of Days, whose name existed before the sun, the symbol portrayed young Joseph, who came into being only yesterday: envied like him, wronged like him by his own people. Thus his whole course ran in the likeness of the Son. Come closer and see that freeborn man who became a slave, as he is sold by members of his household, the sons of slave women. They take from him the provisions he brought and insult him. He goes away as a slave and arrives in Egypt. Though he was a free man, he fought with the Egyptian woman inside the chamber. He went into prison, a captive confined with rebels, and he freed prisoners by interpreting dreams and brought them out. He went up and sat in a chariot, for he was a free man, and he gave abundance and sustenance to the whole world. His enemies came, along with those who had sold him, and fell before him. They were humbled by that unconquered greatness. Turn now and see our Lord, wronged by those who crucified him: he healed the sick and drove out demons, yet they insulted him. They sold him too, received his price, and took him inside and imprisoned him. They brought him out and judged him, seized him, bound him, stretched him out, and crucified him. They had their fill of killing him, took him down, and buried him; but he burst forth. He conquered Sheol, tore down its walls, and ascended from it. He freed the prisoners who were there and brought them out. Instead of a chariot, a cloud became a vehicle of light, and the people saw the buried one exalted in the heights of the air. From the very depth of lowliness came that greatness, so that Joseph’s path would not differ from Christ’s. Let us now say why they did not recognize him— Joseph’s brothers—on that first journey when they came and saw his face. At the later, second revelation they knew who he was, but at the first they did not recognize him, as a mystery required. His being a figure of the Son did not allow him to reveal himself, except on the second occasion when his brothers saw his glory. That first occasion corresponds to that of the Son when he rode in the clouds: no one perceived him, and they did not recognize him as he was exalted. For on that later journey they recognized him and were ashamed before him. That final coming is kept in reserve to be revealed through it. Joseph did not wish to reveal himself to his brothers until they had gathered all together and come to him in that land. One was missing, and he did not reveal himself until that one came. This corresponds to the Son: he gathers the worlds and then reveals himself. But when all the worlds have gathered, his revelation will shine forth. Those who crucified him will be ashamed, just as Joseph’s brothers were put to shame. “I am Joseph, whom you sold to the Egyptians.” Perhaps it will be said, “I am Jesus, whom you crucified.” I recount the things that have passed as they took place, but concerning the things that are to come I will remain silent, since they are kept in reserve. The story of the Son resembles a sea without bounds. Blessed is he who granted Joseph to be a figure of his Son.
The Tenth Discourse, on Joseph
The Tenth Discourse, on Joseph, and on his father and his brothers when he went down to Egypt

Once again, O rich one, bring out and give me from your treasury choice coins for the crown of the discourse about Joseph the pure. Not for my sake, my Lord, should you give me what I have asked of you. For his sake, let my speech grow great, so that I may recount his beautiful qualities. Grant me to complete the discourse of mysteries that is my task concerning him, for in every circumstance you are the giver to whoever asks you. Through you, my Lord, I have traveled Joseph’s path among the Egyptians; through you, let my speech once again richly contend with his story. He brought your mysteries into the world and triumphed because of you. Give me words, so that I may speak of him again. A mystery touched him, and beauty was sprinkled upon him from you. The world has labored to portray his beauty, but it has not been exhausted. Nor have I undertaken to exhaust the account of him. For who could ever measure the sea in the hollow of his hand? Perhaps it would be better for me to keep silent about him and leave him unspoken of, so that no one may think that he has been fully described by what I have said. Truth is my witness that I did not promise to finish; from the beginning, this has been my declaration: I am not capable. For my tongue had no strength to speak of the full extent of this subject, which cannot be told except through our Lord. His beauties are exalted, and his way is great—who can do him justice? For the Son of God was clearly portrayed in him [?]. A beloved child, a delightful youth, a pure man—a sea of words for whom tens of thousands of mouths are not enough. He gazed at God, and his soul was filled with light from him; for his sake, he did not hate his enemies. That discerning man fed those who had sold him during the famine. So that the servant might resemble his master in every way, Joseph possessed compassion and a good heart, and he did not know how to bear a grudge against anyone who hated him. He was pure and serene, a lover of peace and full of love; there was never any room for anger in his soul. Joseph was gentle and humble in heart, acting with discernment; the high position he held did not make him proud. He wished to make himself known to his brothers humbly, so that they would not be terrified by the height of his power. “I am Joseph, whom you sold to the Egyptians.” This was not to reproach them, but to remind them and establish the truth. He sent everyone out so that they would not be exposed before others. He spoke softly and gently, just between himself and them. It was fitting for him, when he gave his brothers clothes, to repay them with good for the evil they had done him. In return for the tunic they had stripped from him, leaving him naked, he gave them all sets of clothes to clothe them. This is the sum of the teaching of the house of God: repay with good the evil done by someone who hates you. His brothers had left Joseph naked in the wilderness, but he peacefully brought out beautiful garments and clothed them. That noble man not only refrained from hating those who hated him; he truly loved them, as it is written. He supplied them with clothes, presents, and costly gifts, as though they had done him good. “For your sake the Lord sent me to the land of the Egyptians,” he told them, to drive away their shame, so that they could look at him without being ashamed of having wronged him. He distanced them from the evil deed they had done, attributing the whole course of events to the Lord: “He sent me,” he said, wisely encouraging those who had sold him. His brothers had sold him, and the Lord had sent him, as he said. Both things were true, and he stated them both: “I am Joseph, whom you sold to the Egyptians. And the Lord sent me for your sake, so that I might feed you.” And it is indeed so: the Lord truly sent him. And it is also so: they had brazenly sold him. The Lord had no part in their deed when they sold him, nor were they aware of, or involved in, the Lord’s sending him. They did evil to Joseph, while the Lord did good. There was one journey, but the two deeds were not mingled in it. They sold him, and he went, but they had no part in his going: theirs alone was the wrongful act of selling him. He went after being sold, but it was not because he had been sold. Rather, the way was arranged by God so that he would go. They sold him without knowing what his going meant. The Lord sent him, but it was not he who sold him when he was sold. They sold him without the Lord, who had no part in it; and the Lord sent him without them, who had no part in it. For the Lord and they were not partners, so that we could say that a single deed was carried out jointly by him and them. They sold him, and the Lord sent him, as it is written. Blame belongs to them, and praise to the Lord, who prepared his way. “The Lord sent me for your sake, to feed you. Go, tell the aged Jacob, so that he may come and see me. Go and say to him, ‘Put away your mourning, great righteous man, for your son is alive and truly longs to see you.’ Hurry, set out, and carry news full of peace, capable of driving prolonged mourning away from the honored man. Run swiftly with the good news to that righteous man, who deserves great consolation. For five years famine will remain throughout the land, with no one sowing or reaping, as has been decreed.” Joseph gave his brothers provisions, as we have said, and sent them to bring his father, as you have heard. As a wise man and a lover of peace, he instructed them, saying, “Do not quarrel on the road as you travel.” This was so that they would not blame one another for what had been done to him, and a sword fall between the brothers on his account. Reuben might say, “Why did you sell him?” And another might repeat, “I said he should not be sold.” Then someone else might say, “Look, what we did to him was a kindness!” The dispute would grow, and there would be room for quarreling. And the journey, full of peace and abundant good news, would proceed amid accusations, disputes, and contention. For this reason he instructed them not to quarrel, so that they would remember his words and refrain from contention. He gave them wagons for the heavy loads of their households, as well as food for the whole journey on which they would come. They took provisions, blessings, and good advice from him, and set out on the road in great peace—hungry men who had eaten their fill. They reached Jacob, eager to deliver the news, each wanting to be the first to bring the good tidings. They came in to the old man, rejoicing and glad. They told him that Joseph was truly alive, but the news was so momentous that he was stunned and did not believe it. Because the news was too much for him, he dismissed it and remained silent. But when they showed him the provisions, the clothes, and everything they had brought, deeds and words compelled him to believe the news he had heard. The pain in his soul over Joseph was like an ulcer, and they came in and bandaged him with good reports. Because it was severe, it had not accepted the first dressing. But they applied reports to it one after another like medicines, and it was healed. He saw the wagons and the large team that Joseph had sent. The old man's spirit was refreshed, and he believed them. He began to drive sorrow away from himself and to take comfort. He put aside his mourning through the report about Joseph that reached his ears. He said, “It is enough for me that Joseph is alive! I will go and see him. Before I die, I will take comfort in him, and then I will depart.” Jacob hurried to go to his beloved. He took his family and set out on the road to Egypt. Love for Joseph was calling him from within Egypt: “Come, old man! Rejoice in your beloved and take comfort in him.” Jacob's journey into Egypt was easy; perhaps there had never been another like it in the whole world. Behind him were famine and the sentence pronounced against Abraham's household; before him were abundance and the love of his son, drawing him onward. Anyone who lovingly inclines his ear toward instruction can benefit from the hidden things concealed within it. The soul is filled with wonder as it understands from it how exalted all the judgments of God are. Here my discourse again asks for greater attention and for love in the soul to open its doors for it to enter. The Lord had pronounced a just sentence against Abraham: his descendants would be enslaved and would labor among foreigners. The Lord told him, “Abram, your descendants will inherit the land.” But his saying, “How will I know?” was a failing. The Lord told him to bring three-year-old sacrificial animals, so that through the offerings he might show him things to come. He commanded him to divide them into pieces, so that through the number of the portions he might teach him about the tribes of his descendants. Abram brought a goat, a ram, and a three-year-old bull, as God had commanded him, and divided them. He placed each piece opposite its companion, as he had been told, and arranged twelve portions on the ground as a symbolic representation. In the offering itself he marked out the tribes and their numbers, and in the Levites he depicted the bird that is free from care. Birds descended upon the pieces, and he drove them away. Through them he depicted the kings of the nations surrounding him. This was to show that his name protects all his descendants and drives armies away from them as he drove away the birds. As the revelation of things to come dawned upon Abraham, justice came to pronounce sentence for his failing. The Just One weighed his words, “How will I know?” and pronounced sentence against him: he would be a slave for four hundred years. For a single thought that flitted through his mind, prompting him to ask, he placed him under bondage for all these years, because he had thought to ask how he would inherit. He subjected his heirs to bondage among foreigners for the years he had decreed. For a single thought the Judge imposed four hundred years; he weighed the matter, issued his decree, and passed judgment justly. For the brief impulse that seized that thought, Abram’s offspring would be enslaved for all these years. This was to make people tremble, so that they would not doubt his promises, and so that no one would ask, concerning anything he says, “How, and by what means?” Let everyone say, “If he subjected Abraham his friend to bondage, who would dare answer him back when he speaks?” For this reason judgment came, and fire with it, to the offering of that righteous man when it was presented. And there was a torch hovering between the divided pieces, and also a furnace of blazing fire beside the offering. Stillness and darkness fell upon Abraham, and in the vision his soul was drawn away from visible things. His mind entered and stood in the realm of hidden things, to see, hear, and understand what was to come. His soul was enlightened, and he learned how he would inherit the land, and that he would be subjected to bondage because he had answered back with a question. The Lord spoke from within the fire to the righteous man: “Know for certain that your offspring will be in bondage. They will serve among foreigners for four hundred years, but I will also judge the nation that enslaves them.” He learned from God not only what he had asked, but something else that he had not wanted to reach his ears. He accepted his sacrifice and hovered over his offering in fire. He showed him how he would inherit the land, as he had wanted to learn. He also showed him that he would be enslaved among foreigners: in a single revelation, the earlier things and the later things. So that no impurity would remain in that honored man’s gold, he polished his soul through a sentence of judgment, so that it would be pure. When the Lord told him, “Your offspring will inherit the land,” his love for that inheritance burned in a fleshly way. That burning desire was a failing in a man such as he, and the Lord removed it from Abraham through a sentence of judgment. As for what the Lord decreed there concerning his enslavement, see how he brought it about through the course of that enslavement. He sent Joseph to be like a household steward in Egypt, to prepare provisions for the offspring of Abraham’s household. After sending him and placing a supply before them, he sent famine and drove them from their dwelling place. And in the place to which he had resolved to bring them, he cleared away the [?], so that they would not be distressed when they went there. He made them hurry to the appointed place of abundance, and they were joyful. So that they would not be distressed at being led into slavery. He was leading them to bind them under the yoke of slaves, while they thought they were being led to freedom. Jacob hurried to go and see his son Joseph, not knowing that they were leading him to become a slave in Egypt. He took his sons, his daughters, and the members of his household as he went down, so that all his offspring, the household of Abraham, would be enslaved. The Lord had already sold them and handed them over; he had made an agreement with their father and subjected them to slavery. So that not one could escape slavery, Jacob took his entire family with him when he went down. Since they had been sold, whether they wished it or not, he gathered them all to go to the land appointed for them. The Lord who had sold them was himself called upon to bring them there, and he wisely arranged the journey so that they would not resist. He took Joseph, Jacob’s very soul, brought him to the land of Egypt, and placed him there. Then he called Jacob to go and see his son. A beloved son, abundant food, and a good land—he set these before him so that he would be enslaved without distress. He opened up Egypt, made it prosperous, and filled it with every luxury; but he gripped the land of Canaan with famine and drove them out. They left their homes without grieving over abandoning them, for famine was hateful, and they set out to move away from it to another land. They went down to Egypt as though it were their own home, for food in abundance and Joseph were as dear to them as their own lives. Who could have compelled old Jacob to move to another land if love for his son Joseph had not led him? The Lord did not wish to distress Jacob, for he was a righteous man and a blessed descendant of the household of Abraham. The Lord had already sold them and handed them over, and the sentence was set down in the book and could not be changed. The Judge of the ages accomplished both things in his wisdom: that Jacob would be enslaved, and that he would not be distressed as he was led away. The king of Egypt, who had been appointed to enslave them, supplied wagons to carry slaves into his land. While he wished to honor them for Joseph’s sake, he was called upon to provide his slaves with transport in which they could be carried. Providence accomplished its purpose on both sides, so that what had been decreed and could not be resisted would be welcomed. So that the king’s heart would not become proud at enslaving them, the secret of their enslavement was hidden from him. And so that they would not grow weary with sorrow on the journey, they did not know where they were being led or for what purpose. If King Pharaoh had brought them as captives, there would have been pride for him and distress for them at being enslaved. Perhaps a remnant might even have escaped captivity, and not all the offspring would have gone down to be enslaved. All the Lord’s judgments are a wonder to those who discern, and in his deeds is the sum of all wisdom. Through famine he brought them out of their homes, and because of Joseph he gave them honor as they were being led along. They called and led one another, and they gathered together. The whole clan went down rejoicing, though it was going to be enslaved. Pharaoh acquired new slaves whom the Lord gave him, but he did not realize that he was being deceived—if only he had realized! Abram’s descendants were being enslaved, as had been decreed, but they did not know the reason for the journey, so that they would not be distressed. The Lord’s providence is beyond human thoughts, and his deeds are an abyss full of wonder. Even the decree he made concerning Abraham, that he would enslave him, he kept until it was brought to light through Abraham’s own descendants. The sons of Israel sold themselves along with their brother, and they enslaved his tender affection and Jacob’s among foreigners. He became the cause and the beginning of the great clan’s laboring [?] in Egypt, as had been decreed. They became the cause of the calamity that was coming and had been prepared by God, so that they would receive suffering from justice. Thus the Lord would be high and exalted above reproach, for he did not enslave them until they themselves gave him a hand in it. The Righteous One had decreed death for Adam because he had sinned, but his sons took the initiative and opened the door for death to enter. He also decreed that Abram’s descendants would be enslaved, but his sons took the initiative: they sold their brother, and then they were enslaved. This is how all evils arise from human beings, for the Lord does not wish to harm humanity. Jacob, then, set out rejoicing and took the road to go and see his son Joseph, as we have said. That honored man hurried because of the news he had heard, eager to go quickly and find comfort with his beloved son. Israel traveled along the road to Egypt with his sons. He reached Beersheba, and the great priest offered sacrifices. At night the Lord granted his revelation to the righteous man, so that he would take courage and continue on the road without anxiety. He appeared to him as a good companion on the road he had taken, and spoke lovingly with him in a vision of the night. The Lord alone is a good friend to his beloved ones: wherever they go, he travels with them to help them. There is no exile for anyone who is close to God, for all regions and lands belong to him. For the earth and everything in it belong to the Lord, as it is written, and there is no place where he is not present for anyone who calls upon him. Even if you had a road by which to pass beyond the world, with the Lord beside you there would be peace there, discerning one. The lands and the regions belong to him. He stays and journeys with his beloved ones, though he does not move. The Lord encouraged Jacob on the road as he traveled to the land of Egypt, so that he would not be distressed at leaving his own country. “Look, I myself am going with you,” he said to him. “I will bring you down, and I will bring you up from Egypt. I will make you into a great nation among the Egyptians.” Jacob heard this and continued on his journey with a glad heart. Israel went down and reached Egypt, where his beloved was. Joseph heard and went out himself to meet his father. They met one another—the grieving old man and the young man who had been driven away. Mourning fled, and the distress that had gripped them passed away. The father’s tender feelings were comforted by his son’s love, and the two beloved ones rejoiced in their own loving encounter. The yearning old man and the radiant young man rejoiced in one another, and with joy they drove away their long-standing distress. The beloved ones, relieved of their troubles, clasped one another. They embraced and kissed each other affectionately. Old Jacob fell upon Joseph’s neck and wept. The young man too wept upon the neck of his righteous father. There was great weeping from their abundant joy, for when natural feeling grows strong, it wells up in tears. His fatherly affection welled up at the sight of his son, and weeping was stirred by the surge of tenderness that overflowed. The day saw the sun, its friend, and longed to meet it; all the light was hidden by its rays. Jacob said, “Now let me die, since I have seen you, my son! When I had no hope, your father’s own soul has welcomed you. Now, even if I die, it is not death for me, for the sight of you has raised me up like resurrection raising a dead man lying prostrate. My son, my hope had been cut off; there was no possibility of seeing you. Yet when I was not expecting it, the Lord granted it to me, and here I have welcomed you. I was dead while still alive because I was deprived of your company. Even if I die, I am alive now because I have seen you. This life was no life when I had lost you. Now that I have found you, it is life, even if I die. Bury me now, for death seems like resurrection to me, since the life I lived before was death to me. My beloved son, life of my life, who will grant me to gaze at you and see you, to be comforted by you and forget my troubles? You dead man who has come to life, who raised you from the grave? For to me you had been in Sheol among the departed for so very long. I asked for your corpse to be returned to me, but no one gave it to me. Mourning for you choked me; in you I will find comfort. For Joseph’s sake, let all the graves bring forth their dead, for he has been returned to me like someone long departed. From now on, may the world see every joy, and may the dead return from the grave to their loved ones. Now that you have come, my beloved, I can go to the grave, for my heart, which was broken because of you, has been comforted. Your sweet fragrance has reached my eyes and given them light.” The light of my being had grown dark because of you. I will go down to Sheol rejoicing that you are not there. I will lie down and rest, knowing that you are among the living. You whom your brothers envied, blessed is he who kept you safe from harm and granted me to see you and find comfort in you when I had no hope. I have forgotten my bitterness; my troubles have passed, and my misfortunes have ended. By seeing you, I have gained every joy from now on. Let no one give up hope that his dead will rise again, for Joseph has returned to me from the grave, so that I may find comfort in him. Israel, the mourning old man, rejoiced at the sight of his son, and Joseph, the beloved young man, was glad to meet his father. Look at the mourning that, a little earlier, had been torment: Joseph was sold, envied, driven away, wronged, and imprisoned. Jacob was mourning, sorrowful, downcast, and full of woes. His mourning was intense, his distress was great, and he endured terrors. He tore his garment, put on sackcloth, and wept bitterly. The young man was enslaved, and the old man was far from comfort. Come, see now: time has passed, the ordeal has ended, and Joseph has triumphed, risen high, ruled, and become great. Jacob’s mourning was changed into heartfelt joy, and his sorrow was turned into gladness. Good things drove away the bad and made them pass, as though they had never existed at all from the beginning. Jacob rejoices, Joseph is glad, and mourning is no more. The things that happened have faded with time and are gone. The wheel turned, swept them away, and they were changed. They had all happened for Joseph’s sake, not against him. The Lord of the ages holds all changes in his hands; their course and their forms belong to him. He brings people low and raises them up according to his will, so that by every means he may bind every mind to himself. He changes the times, both of lowliness and of greatness, so that the world may trust in him alone and not in the times. He gives wealth and poverty, so that through both the world may learn that he brings about change through his deeds. He strikes and heals, so that whoever is struck may take refuge in him, for there is a bandage for all the pains that afflict him. He left Jacob sitting in mourning while keeping in store for him that great comfort at the end: the sight of his son. He established his testimony in the young Joseph when he was sold, and concealed the mystery from his father for a purpose. When he had carried out through him the whole course of things to come, he called him and gave him back to his father, so that he might find comfort in him before dying. He borrowed him from his father for a little while and portrayed his mysteries through him. When all his foreshadowings had been fulfilled, he gave him back to his father. He stole the young man away and sent him on a journey without his father. When his work had reached its completion, he revealed to his father where he was. He faithfully guarded the trust that had been placed with him. He made use of it and completed his work without being dishonored. He received a slave from the pit when he was sold, and gave back a free man, exalted and seated in a chariot. He took a poor man, envied and hated, from among his brothers. And he gave back a rich man before whom masters bow down. He brought him, and he entered naked; and because he worked there for a little while, He clothed himself in the glory of Egypt and returned to his aged father. I will now leave off telling this unfathomable story, Confessing that the story of the Hebrew man has overcome me. It is not that the discourse has reached its end; rather, I have been overcome. Blessed is he whose deeds cannot be comprehended by those on earth.
The tenth discourse on Joseph, composed by the blessed Mar Jacob the Teacher, is finished.
